chunks.content: 1 Introduction Soccer is one of the most popular sports worldwide and is a contact sport in which players are at risk of head injuries and concussions ( , ). The reported incidence of concussions is 0.27–0.41 per 1,000 athletic exposures for school-aged girls and 0.17–0.19 per 1,000 athletic exposures for school-aged boys ( , ). Head injuries can result from contact between the head and another player's head or body parts, the ground, a goal post, or head-to-ball contact ( , , ). A concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a direct blow to the head, neck, or another part of the body ( ). A concussive injury triggers a cascade of molecular alterations, including elevated neurotransmitter release, altered ion flux, hyperglycolysis, and various other metabolic shifts. These complex metabolic disturbances can result in either transient or prolonged neurological deficits. Consequently, concussions must be identified immediately to prevent subsequent injury and mitigate the risk of persistent symptoms ( ). Any athlete suspected of sustaining a concussion must be immediately (on field) evaluated using a standardized tool i.e., CFRP which includes validated modified Maddock's questions to explore orientation and memory. Furthermore, the injured player should be withdrawn from play, monitored for worsening effects, and be encouraged to rest until asymptomatic ( – ). Any athlete suspected of sustaining a concussion must undergo an immediate on-field evaluation using a standardized tool, such as the Concussion Fast Recognition Protocol (CFRP). This protocol includes validated Modified Maddocks Questions (MMQ) designed to assess orientation and memory. Furthermore, the injured player must be withdrawn from play, monitored for any worsening of symptoms, and encouraged to rest until they are completely asymptomatic ( – ). Based on the preceding data, the CFRP was utilized for the current study. However, it is important to note that the CFRP is not sport-specific and has not yet been validated in Spanish-speaking populations. While the CFRP has previously been used to identify concussions in soccer players, there are currently no data to validate its application in children ( – ). Furthermore, the Maddocks questions are primarily intended for the on-field evaluation of athletes aged 12 years and older who do not present with obvious signs of concussion ( ). The primary objective of this study is to determine the minimum age at which the Modified Maddocks Questions (MMQ) can be reliably applied to soccer players, facilitating the future validation of the Concussion Fast Recognition Protocol (CFRP) in children. We hypothesized that 1) Both comprehension and response accuracy would increase with age across the 4–8-year range. 2) Questions involving the recall of past events would yield lower accuracy compared to orientation-based questions, even among non-concussed children. 2 Methods We conducted an observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study among youth soccer players in Montevideo, Uruguay, using an adapted version of the Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT). The study took place between July and October 2024. Following authorization from the Secretaria Nacional de Deporte and approval from the respective club academies, participating teams were selected via random sampling. All participants remained anonymous throughout the process. 2.1 Participant selection and criteria Athletes were eligible if they were between the ages of 4 and 8, reflecting the early entry age for organized soccer in Uruguay ( ). Exclusion criteria consisted of: Pre-existing neurocognitive deficits. Suspected or confirmed concussion sustained during the match prior to testing. Lack of parental/guardian informed consent or player assent. 2.2 Data collection and administration The MMQT was administered orally by trained investigators during the halftime break to evaluate baseline cognitive function, attention, and comprehension in a non-injured population. To ensure objectivity, the investigators maintained no prior relationship with the participating clubs. Each assessment lasted between 1 and 3 min. If a child provided an incorrect response, the question was reformulated to further assess their capacity for comprehension vs. simple misinterpretation. Data, including gender, age, and club affiliation, were recorded in an electronic spreadsheet. Responses to each of the five MMQT questions were classified as either correct or incorrect. 2.3 Statistical analysis For data processing, participants were stratified into one-year age intervals. For each age group, we calculated the proportion of correct vs. incorrect responses and evaluated the overall comprehension levels for each of the five specific MMQT items ( ). 2.4 Ethical statement The study protocol and informed consent procedures were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the School of Medicine at the University of the Republic, Uruguay. 2.5 Patient and public involvement Given the study design, patient and public involvement (PPI) was not required during the planning or execution phases of this research. 2.6 Statistical analysis To examine the association between age and both MMQT response accuracy (correct vs. incorrect) and question comprehension (understood vs. not understood), we employed either the Chi-square ( χ 2) test or Fisher's exact

In cases where significant associations were detected, post-hoc pairwise comparisons of proportions were performed. To account for multiple comparisons and reduce the risk of Type I errors, p -values were adjusted using the Bonferroni correction ( ). We also evaluated the association between age and the MMQT variables using logistic regression models, with age as the predictor and each question as a separate binary dependent variable. To estimate the probability of false negative or false positive outcomes based on the number of incorrect responses, we employed a binomial distribution. This calculation assumed independence between responses and utilized the mean probability of an incorrect answer across the questionnaire. The internal consistency of the MMQT was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha. In doing so, we acknowledged that the tool was originally developed as a brief clinical screening instrument rather than a unidimensional psychometric scale. Given the exploratory and descriptive nature of this study, no formal a priori sample size calculation was performed. Instead, the sample size was determined pragmatically based on participant availability and feasibility during the study period. The final cohort ( n = 88) was deemed sufficient to estimate comprehension and response accuracy with acceptable precision across the target age range. With this sample, proportions near 90% could be estimated with a margin of error of approximately ±6%–7%. Additionally, this sample size provided approximately 80% power to detect a moderate effect size (Cramer's V ≈ 0,30) in the chi-square analyses. Statistical analyses were performed using JASP (version 0.18.3). For all tests, a p -value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 Results The study involved 88 males, aged 4 to 8 years, from six different youth soccer clubs. The distribution of children by age was as follows: 1 child aged 4, 9 children aged 5, 23 children aged 6, 33 children aged 7, and 22 children aged 8. Although all youth soccer clubs in Montevideo accept both sexes, within the age ranges chosen for the study, none of the randomly selected teams had girls on their roster. summarizes the proportion of children who correctly answered and understood each Modified Maddocks Question (MMQ) by age group. Fisher's exact test revealed no statistically significant association between age and either the accuracy of responses or comprehension of questions. Similar findings were obtained using logistic regression models with age as a predictor. However, results should be interpreted cautiously due to the small number of participants in the 4- and 5-year-old groups. When considering the total number of correct responses (range 0-5), the Spearman correlation between age and total score was 0,193 (95% CI: −0,017; 0.387), indicating no association. Conclusions cannot be generalized to 4-year-olds based on the single participant in that group. In contrast, comprehension rates were similar across all questions. The proportion of correct responses to question 4 was significantly lower compared to the other questions ( ). This suggests it may be more difficult or less clearly understood. Internal consistency of the five MMQT items was explored using Cronbach's alpha. The overall alpha coefficient was 0,668 (95% CI: 0.556; 0.779), indicating moderate internal consistency. When Question 4 was excluded, Cronbach's alpha decreased to 0,561, suggesting that this item did not reduce overall scale coherence. If the child is removed from the field after one incorrect answer, the probability of error (removing the child without a concussion) is 1 in 2.5. The probability of error decreases significantly if the child provides an increasing number of incorrect answers ( ). 4 Discussion Reports of sports-related concussions, particularly in soccer, have increased in prevalence over the last decade. This trend is likely driven by enhanced diagnostic surveillance, heightened public awareness, and targeted education for parents, coaches, and athletes. Furthermore, the rising competitiveness of youth soccer has contributed to higher injury rates ( ). Among school-aged children, it is estimated that over 50% of concussions occur during recreational play ( ). In most competitive settings, certified athletic trainers serve as the primary responders for the initial assessment and management of these injuries. In recreational sports settings, however, it is essential that parents and coaches possess the necessary knowledge to recognize concussion symptoms ( ). The Concussion Fast Recognition Protocol (CFRP), implemented in 2014, was originally designed for adult athletes; consequently, there remains a lack of data regarding its utility and efficacy in pediatric populations ( ). Our findings indicate no significant association between the three primary parameters investigated: age, auditory comprehension, and the frequency of correct responses. Notably, most of the study population consisted of children aged 6, 7, and 8 years, with a smaller representation of younger participants (one 4-year-old and nine 5-year-olds). Crucially, no statistically significant differences in performance were observed among the children in the 6–8 age range. Across all age groups, participants demonstrated a high degree of language comprehension (≥96%), providing correct answers in most instances. However, Question 4 consistently yielded incorrect responses across the cohort. This finding suggests that Question 4 may be unsuitable for this specific age group; we recommend its exclusion from the protocol should further studies confirm these preliminary results. Consequently, any child failing to provide a correct response to the remaining items should be managed with a high degree of clinical suspicion and, as a precautionary measure, removed from play for formal medical assessment and rest. The Maddocks questions were originally developed for professional Australian rules football players. The initial 14-item tool assessed orientation and recent memory and was typically administered within 10 min of a suspected concussion or upon the patient regaining consciousness ( , , ). Historically, and consistent with our observations regarding Question 4, items evaluating recent memory have proven more sensitive in distinguishing between concussed and non-concussed athletes, whereas questions assessing remote events often proved challenging for all players, regardless of injury status ( , ). To the best of our knowledge, there are no published reports on the Spanish validation of the Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT) for young children, although it is a recognized instrument for differentiating between concussed and non-concussed adolescents and adults during the acute phase of injury. Since its inception in 2005, the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) has undergone several revisions, consistently including the Maddocks questions as a core component ( ). However, research has highlighted significant performance variations linked to demographic variables, as well as cultural and linguistic differences ( , , ). While the SCAT is a standardized tool with universal applicability across disciplines including soccer, hockey, basketball, and American football, its development and validation have been most robustly established within rugby ( – ). It is therefore critical to recognize that a literal translation of the SCAT may be inadequate; cultural and linguistic adaptations are essential to ensure effective communication and prevent clinical misunderstandings ( ). It is therefore critical to recognize that a literal translation of the SCAT may be inadequate; cultural and linguistic adaptations are essential to ensure effective communication and prevent clinical misunderstandings ( ). The impact of language on concussion evaluation in youth athletes remains poorly understood ( ). Studies utilizing the Child SCAT5 have found that Spanish-speaking children even when evaluated in English reported fewer symptoms and performed worse on specific subtests compared to their English-speaking peers. These discrepancies may be attributed to social determinants of health, such as socioeconomic status and acculturation, or inherent psychometric limitations of the tool. This underscores the need for pediatric concussion instruments to account for cultural and linguistic nuances to ensure diagnostic validity ( ). Notably, while the MMQT has been validated in Chinese, Arabic, and Italian within various SCAT versions, a Spanish pediatric validation remains a critical gap ( – ). Athletic trainers and specialized healthcare personnel are in short supply in child sports. Therefore, it is necessary to raise awareness and provide training on the use of CRT6 to all adults supervising child/adolescent sports. The CRT6 created by the Concussion in Sport Group (CISG) has been translated into several languages ( ). This study supports the utility of a Spanish-adapted MMQT for concussion screening in children aged 5–8 years. Comprehension was consistently high across age groups, although the ability to answer correctly was variable especially for questions involving recall of past events (e.g., Question 4). Previous studies on the original Maddock questions have similarly reported that items involving recall of past events are less discriminative and more variable, even among older athletes ( ). In contrast, orientation-based questions (e.g., field, half of match) rely on immediate contextual awareness and appear more robust across age groups. Given the lower performance on Question 4 despite high comprehension, its exclusion from the MMQT for this age group is recommended. While the study was limited to male athletes and had limited representation among 4- and 5-year-olds, the results are promising. Future research should expand validation to girls, younger children, and other sports. Given the limited availability of trained medical staff at youth sports events, tools like MMQT must be easily understood by non-medical adults (e.g., parents, coaches) and appropriately adapted to cultural and linguistic contexts. 4.1 Clinical implications Identifying concussions in the pediatric population remains a formidable diagnostic challenge, largely due to the communication barriers inherent to early cognitive development and a paucity of validated assessment tools. In this context, the present study offers novel and clinically significant evidence by demonstrating the feasibility of the Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT) for use among Spanish-speaking children aged 5 to 8 years. 4.2 Limitations This study is subject to several limitations. First, the sample consisted exclusively of male participants, as the randomly selected teams within the target age range lacked female players; consequently, these findings may not be generalizable to female athletes. Second, the younger cohorts were underrepresented comprising only one 4-year-old and nine 5-year-olds which limits the strength of the conclusions for these specific age groups. Third, the relatively small, convenience-based sample size may have reduced statistical power, particularly for subgroup analyses. Furthermore, the cross-sectional design and administration of the MMQT in a non-concussed setting during halftime may not fully capture the ecological validity of actual sideline conditions following a head injury. The practice of reformulating incorrect answers to assess comprehension, while helpful, may have introduced a degree of researcher subjectivity. Finally, as the MMQT has not been formally validated in Spanish-speaking pediatric populations, cultural or contextual factors may further limit its broader application. Future research incorporating larger, more diverse cohorts is warranted. 5 Conclusions Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT) is a feasible sideline concussion screening instrument for Spanish-speaking male athletes aged 5 to 8 years. However, due to its consistently lower accuracy in this demographic, we recommend that Question 4 be excluded from routine use. Clinically, any child who provides one or more incorrect responses should be immediately removed from play and referred for a comprehensive medical evaluation.

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Blood-based biomarkers such as glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) and NFL are used to detect acute neural injury after sport-related concussion, yet limited research has examined preseason baseline concentrations in contact or collision sport athletes or potential sex differences. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Female collegiate contact and collision sport athletes demonstrated higher baseline GFAP and NFL concentrations than males, whereas ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 and total tau did not differ by sex. Exposure-related variables, such as age of first exposure and time since most recent concussion, were not associated with biomarker levels. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings identify biological sex as a source of variability in select brain-derived biomarkers and suggest that sex should be considered in future biomarker validation and longitudinal research. Introduction Repetitive head impacts (RHI) are head impacts that do not result in the clinical diagnostic criteria of concussion but may trigger complex cellular and molecular processes that evolve following the initial or repeated exposure. In recent years, there has been growing concern that exposure to RHI is detrimental to long-term neurological health and linked to functional deficits such as blood-brain barrier dysfunction, abnormal neurometabolic responses, aggregation of tau or amyloid protein, increased risk of developing chronic traumatic encephalopathy, depression and other symptoms. Unfortunately, RHI exposure is a standard component of both contact and collision sport participation, ranging from hundreds to thousands of impacts over the course of a season, depending on the position and level of play. This is especially concerning considering that fewer than 2000 RHI have been associated, in a dose-response relationship, with later-life neurological deficits. RHI and its possible link to traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES), the clinical disorder related to neuropathologically diagnosed chronic traumatic encephalopathy, has also received recent attention. One of the four diagnostic criteria for TES is substantial exposure to RHI’s (ie, a minimum of 5 years of organised contact/collision sport, with at least two of those years occurring at the high school level or beyond). The potential societal and economic implications of RHI are significant. Therefore, we must seek objective measures to detect early changes caused by career RHI. Previously, an earlier age of first exposure to contact/collision sports (<12 years of age) was proposed as causing later life neurodegeneration ; however, these early studies were not able to be replicated. Thus, within the current TES consensus statement, career duration is the only modifiable risk factor. Young physically active athletes may have sufficient cognitive reserves, compensatory neurocognitive capabilities or neural plasticity to adapt and overcome potential RHI-related neurotrauma. Further, the forces generated by younger athletes may not be sufficient to initiate the neurometabolic, anatomic or other injury mechanisms. Clinical measures (eg, neurocognition, balance) often fail to detect meaningful group-level differences in clinical performance or symptom presentation in collegiate contact/collision sport athletes during baseline testing. In contrast, neuroimaging studies have demonstrated RHI-related alterations in brain structure and function even in young athletes. Inflammation plays a vital role in both the repair and neurodegenerative processes following RHI; however, it can be challenging to characterise due to the invasive nature, cost and limited feasibility of direct central nervous system assessment in active athletes. Peripheral blood samples provide meaningful information about neuroinflammation in a safe, cost-effective manner. Several brain-derived biomarkers (BDM), including glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP), NFL, ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) and total tau, have successfully identified the course of neuronal, axonal and astroglial damage following concussion. RHI may worsen these processes by priming microglial cells, leading to an exaggerated inflammatory reaction on subsequent head trauma. Chronic inflammation from RHI exposure can potentially exacerbate neuronal injury, causing further degeneration and resulting in a more significant accumulation of neurofibrillar tangles and amyloid plaques, both of which may be related to neurodegenerative diseases. While amyloid and tau accumulation are established in Alzheimer’s disease, their relevance to RHI-related changes in young athletes remains unclear and speculative at this stage. In this context, baseline serum concentrations of GFAP, NFL, total tau and UCH-L1 may offer insight into individual biological sensitivity to head impact exposure, even in the absence of overt concussion symptoms. Sex differences have been documented in both concussion and neurocognitive disorders. Females who experience RHI may have poorer executive function and an elevated risk of depression compared with non-contact athletes. In later life, women are at increased risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases independent of RHI exposure, supporting underlying neurophysiological sex differences. Despite these concerning neurobehavioural and pathological findings in females, current RHI literature focuses primarily on clinical data, with later-life samples largely consisting of former male collision sport athletes. In later life, women are at increased risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases independent of RHI exposure, supporting underlying neurophysiological sex differences. Despite these concerning neurobehavioural and pathological findings in females, current RHI literature focuses primarily on clinical data, with later-life samples largely consisting of former male collision sport athletes. Sex differences in biomarkers may advance our understanding of injury heterogeneity and the complexity of RHI and reveal sex-dependent pathobiological processes and disease mechanisms. Many consequences of RHI remain to be elucidated, including objective measures in current athletes and stronger consideration of sex differences. Therefore, the purpose of this study is twofold: (1) to examine whether serum concentrations of four brain-derived biomarkers (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau) differ by biological sex while accounting for exposure-related variables, including age of first exposure (AFE) to contact sports and time since most recent concussion, and (2) to evaluate whether AFE and time since concussion are associated with biomarker concentrations in a subsample of collegiate football athletes. We hypothesised that serum concentrations of brain-derived biomarkers would differ by biological sex, with females exhibiting higher levels than males and that exposure-related variables, including an earlier age of first exposure and shorter time since most recent concussion, would be associated with elevated biomarker concentrations. Material and methods This cross-sectional study was a secondary analysis from the multicentre, prospective study conducted by the National Collegiate Athletic Association and the US Department of Defense Concussion Assessment, Research and Education (CARE) Consortium at the six CARE Advanced Research Core sites, including the US Military and Air Force Academies between 14 October 2014 and 30 August 2018. The Medical College of Wisconsin Institutional Review Board (IRB) and the local IRB and Human Research Protection Office at each performance site reviewed and approved all study procedures. All potential participants provided written informed consent. The inclusion criteria were incoming male and female athletes participating in contact and collision sports. Exclusion criteria included a current concussion diagnosis. A lifetime history of concussion did not exclude participants. A total of 700 college athletes (male=548/700, 78.3%) were included in the analysis ( ). Patient and public involvement Former collegiate athletes were consulted during the parent CARE Consortium study to provide input on study design and data collection logistics. Patients or members of the public were not involved in the conduct, reporting or dissemination plans specific to this secondary analysis. The detailed procedures for demographic information and blood sample acquisition have been previously described. Briefly, following participants’ consent at preseason baseline testing, non-fasting blood samples were collected by venipuncture. Using a 10 mL red top Serum Tube (Becton Dickinson, New Jersey, USA), samples were left to clot and centrifuged at 1,500 g for 15 min within 60 min of collection. Next, samples were aliquoted and stored at −80°C until shipment on dry ice to a central repository. Biomarker serum levels were quantified using the Quanterix Simoa (Lexington, Massachusetts, USA) Neuro 4-Plex B (N4PB) multiplex assay, which simultaneously measured GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau concentrations. At present, there are no established clinical thresholds or reference cut-offs for ‘elevated’ or ‘reduced’ concentrations of GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 or total tau in healthy or asymptomatic athletic populations; therefore, BDM concentrations were interpreted as relative to group differences rather than absolute clinical significance. Age of first exposure to contact or collision sports The AFE was calculated based on participants’ self-reports of when they began participating in contact or collision sports. If an athlete participated in multiple contact or collision sports concurrently, AFE was defined as the earliest age at which they began participating in any of these sports. Cumulative years of exposure were not double-counted across multiple sports. Sport was categorised based on the primary contact or collision sport in which the athlete was actively participating as a collegiate student-athlete at the time of baseline testing. Although many participants reported prior participation in multiple contact or collision sports, exposure history from earlier sport participation was captured through AFE, which reflected the earliest age at which the athlete began participating in any contact or collision sport. For example, if an athlete began playing soccer at age 6 and football at age 8, with both sports played through age 18, their AFE was recorded as six. AFE was included as a continuous variable in all general linear models. To address our primary aim, a series of general linear models were conducted separately for each neuroinflammatory biomarker (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau). Statistical analyses Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarise participant characteristics, including biological sex, age, sport, concussion history, AFE and time since most recent concussion. To address our primary aim, a series of general linear models were conducted separately for each neuroinflammatory biomarker (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau). Each model included biological sex, sport (ie, hockey, soccer, lacrosse, rugby), AFE, time since most recent concussion (days) and a sex-by-sport interaction term as independent variables. Effect sizes were reported using partial eta squared (η²), with benchmarks for small (0.01), medium (0.06) and large (0.14) effects. To address our second aim, separate univariate regression models were conducted within the subsample of football athletes. These models assessed whether AFE or time since their most recent concussion was associated with biomarker concentrations. Given that American football has been shown to involve particularly high cumulative exposure to repetitive head impacts relative to other contact and collision sports, and because exposure characteristics vary widely by position and individual participation patterns, we conducted a secondary subgroup analysis of football athletes to evaluate exposure-related associations within this sport specifically. This subgroup analysis complements our broader examination across all sports without implying that football is the primary focus of the study. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, V.29.0 (IBM, Armonk, New York, USA). Statistical significance was defined a priori at α=0.05. Adjusted R ² values were reported to reflect model fit and account for the number of predictors in each model. Biomarker distributions were visually inspected prior to analysis. Based on inspection of distributions and residual plots, biomarker concentrations were analysed on their original scale. Model assumptions of linearity, normality of residuals and homoscedasticity were evaluated and deemed acceptable for the present analyses. Formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was not applied. All analyses were specified a priori and focused on biologically distinct biomarkers that reflect different cellular and injury-related processes rather than multiple tests of a single outcome. Applying conservative corrections across these outcomes would substantially increase the risk of type II error. Accordingly, results were interpreted cautiously, with emphasis placed on effect sizes and consistency of findings across biomarkers rather than statistical significance alone. Results Aim 1: Sex and exposure-related differences in biomarkers Across the full sample of contact and collision sport athletes, sex significantly predicted GFAP and NFL concentrations. Females exhibited higher serum GFAP ( F 1,113 =15.88, p<0.001, η²=0.123) and NFL ( F 1,113 =4.92, p=0.029, η²=0.042) levels than males ( ). The overall model explained a relatively small proportion of variance in GFAP (adjusted R ²=0.069) and NFL (adjusted R ²=0.051). No significant main effects were observed for sport, AFE or time since most recent concussion for either biomarker. Interaction effects (sex×sport) were also non-significant. For UCH-L1 and total tau, sex, sport and AFE did not reach statistical significance ( and 4). The models explained minimal variance (UCH-L1: adjusted R ²=–0.023; total tau: adjusted R ²=–0.012). Aim 2: Football-Specific Exposure Associations Univariate regression models revealed no significant associations between biomarker concentrations and either AFE or time since the most recent concussion. Across all four biomarkers (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1, total tau), model fits were poor ( R ² range=0.004–0.027), with adjusted R ² values near or below zero. Discussion The effects of RHI across a career have primarily been examined in older male former football players or healthy young collegiate athletes using clinical measures ; however, neuroimaging studies in current contact and collision sport athletes have also demonstrated RHI-related alterations in brain structure and function. Accordingly, the present study investigated objective blood-derived biomarkers in a diverse sample of active athletes without a current concussion. The primary finding of this study was that female student-athletes had significantly higher BDM serum concentrations of NFL and GFAP than their male counterparts, independent of AFE and time since the most recent concussion. Results from our study do not support a relationship between AFE and BDM serum concentration in a sample of apparently healthy young adults. Although prior studies examining career duration have reported limited associations with clinical outcomes among current athletes, the present findings extend this literature by demonstrating that sex-based differences in blood-derived biomarkers are evident even when exposure is operationalised by age at first exposure and time since the most recent concussion rather than by career duration. Although this study examined exposure-related factors, it is important to emphasise that the variables used (ie, AFE, sport category and time since most recent concussion) are indirect and relatively coarse proxies for cumulative RHI exposure. These metrics do not capture the substantial heterogeneity in head impact frequency, magnitude, position-specific exposure or duration across and within sports. As such, the absence of associations between these exposure-related variables and biomarker concentrations may not fully reflect the complex relationship between RHI exposure and biological outcomes. Despite women making up approximately 44% of all college athletes, females remain a largely understudied group in head trauma research. Our finding of significantly higher NFL and GFAP serum concentrations in female athletes suggests a potentially different underlying biological response to RHI. However, the relatively modest R 2 values (UCH-L1: adjusted R ²=–0.023; total tau: adjusted R ²=–0.012) indicate that these predictors account for only a small proportion of the variance, underscoring the need for further investigation before strong conclusions can be made. Notably, the low explained variance across models underscores that baseline biomarker concentrations are influenced by factors beyond those captured in the present analyses. GFAP is an intermediate filament protein expressed in astrocytes and serves as a marker of glial activation, particularly in response to neuroinflammatory or neurodegenerative processes. NFL, a structural component of the neuronal cytoskeleton, is released into circulation following axonal injury and is often elevated in response to trauma, vascular insult and neurodegeneration. Female sex has been associated with health disparities following a concussion, with some studies reporting females to have worse recovery outcomes, more symptoms, greater symptom severity, performed worse on neurocognitive tests, larger deficits in motor coordination, worse locomotive functioning and vestibular reflexes and took longer to recover from their concussion than males. However, it is important to note that other studies have found no significant sex differences in the clinical presentation or recovery outcome following concussion between the sexes. Sex-based differences may influence RHI-related outcomes, with potential factors including hormonal status, contraceptive use, menstrual cycle phase and lower cervical muscle strength in females. Detecting sex-specific long-term changes in BDM serum concentrations could provide researchers and clinicians with early insight into the identification of neurodegenerative diseases, further highlighting the need to investigate sex as a biological variable in long-term health outcomes from RHI. We found serum GFAP and NFL concentrations to be significantly elevated in female athletes compared with males, independent of sport, AFE and time since the most recent concussion. These findings highlight the need for future work to determine whether sex-specific reference ranges or thresholds are appropriate, particularly in longitudinal or outcome-linked studies. Interestingly, while some studies in older adults have reported higher NFL concentrations in males, our data from young, currently active athletes demonstrate the opposite pattern. This discrepancy may reflect age-related, hormonal or exposure-based differences in biomarker expression, further emphasising the importance of considering sex and chronological age when evaluating blood-based indicators of neurotrauma. Although females exhibited higher baseline GFAP and NFL concentrations, these findings may not fully reflect the complex relationship between RHI and neurobiological outcomes. Elevated baseline biomarker levels may reflect sex differences in normative biomarker physiology, including differences in body composition, blood volume, hormonal status, clearance kinetics or assay behaviour, rather than injury-related processes. Additionally, the absence of a non-contact female comparison group limits our ability to determine whether observed differences are sport-related or reflect broader sex-based physiological differences. Accordingly, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive and hypothesis-generating, warranting further investigation using appropriate control groups and longitudinal designs. Female athletes in our cohort reported an AFE almost 2 years earlier than their male counterparts, which may reflect a longer duration of exposure to contact and collision sport participation; however, patterns of head impact exposure and concussion risk differ by sport. Although extended exposure could theoretically increase vulnerability to neurodegenerative diseases, women typically do not participate in football, which accounts for the majority of head impacts, sport-related concussion (SRC) and an overwhelming percentage of the documented cases of neurodegenerative diseases. In our analysis, AFE, UCH-L1 and total tau were not significantly influenced by any of the predictors examined. Notably, the very low adjusted R ² values observed in the football subgroup analyses indicate limited explained variance, and these football-specific models should therefore be interpreted with caution and viewed as exploratory rather than definitive evidence of exposure–biomarker relationships. The absence of effects for UCH-L1 and total tau may reflect their shorter post-injury temporal windows, reduced sensitivity to cumulative subconcussive exposure or greater variability in expression across individuals. In our analysis, AFE, UCH-L1 and total tau were not significantly influenced by any of the predictors examined. Notably, the very low adjusted R ² values observed in the football subgroup analyses indicate limited explained variance, and these football-specific models should therefore be interpreted with caution and viewed as exploratory rather than definitive evidence of exposure–biomarker relationships. The absence of effects for UCH-L1 and total tau may reflect their shorter post-injury temporal windows, reduced sensitivity to cumulative subconcussive exposure or greater variability in expression across individuals. Sports-related concussion is associated with elevated BDM markers in the acute post-injury phase ; however, how these markers change over the course of a lifetime with RHI exposure remains unclear. Moreover, the combined effect of concussion history and cumulative RHI on BDM, rather than each factor alone, is still unknown. Based on the promising evidence that BDM may support the early detection, prognosis and monitoring of neurodegeneration in later life, future research should investigate how serum concentrations change with ageing and how they correlate with clinical diagnoses of neurodegenerative diseases. Consistent with our findings, prior studies have not observed significant associations between AFE and clinical outcomes. These AFE studies, based on four independent cohorts with nearly 10 000 young adult athletes across 20 outcome measures, found no meaningful relationships in clinical outcomes. To the best of our knowledge, no published studies of current athletes show a statistically significant association between AFE and worse functional or clinical outcomes following concussion. The current study yielded similar findings, in which we derived AFE from the total number of athletic seasons self-reported by athletes. Overall, we did not observe a significant relationship between AFE and BDM in current college athletes. However, the extent to which RHI, biomarkers and biological sex are related throughout the lifespan remains to be elucidated. Limitations The participants in this study were part of the Advanced Research Core of the CARE Consortium, which resulted in an unequal representation of sexes and sports. Indeed, nearly 50% of our sample consisted of football players, and there was no equivalent female collision sport comparison. However, an important strength of this study is the inclusion of male and female rugby athletes, one of the few contact sports in which the rules and contact demands are similar across sexes, allowing for more comparable examination of repetitive head impact exposure between males and females. The absence of a non-contact female control group limits direct comparisons and reduces our ability to distinguish collision-related effects from baseline sex differences. Additionally, the use of proxy measures for exposure introduces the potential for exposure misclassification, and residual confounding from unmeasured factors may have influenced observed associations. We only measured BDM serum concentrations at a single preseason time point; subsequent assessments at various time points and additional biomarkers should be considered, particularly across the lifespan and account for menstrual cycle fluctuations in premenopausal women. Future research is needed, using different populations and methodologies to better understand whether RHI is associated with differences in brain physiology or functioning, along with compensatory strategies, in the years to decades following contact and collision sports careers. Specifically, research is needed to examine the association between RHI and both clinical (eg, neurocognitive function, balance, symptom severity) and objective (eg, BDM, neuroimaging) measures across the lifespan in both men and women. Blood samples were taken from a convenience sample, and participants were not enrolled with the purpose of equal representation across all sports. Conclusion Females currently participating in contact and collision sports have significantly higher GFAP and NFL serum concentrations independent of sport, AFE and time since most recent concussion. These results underscore sex-based differences in biological sensitivity to head impact exposure and may inform future biomarker surveillance frameworks, particularly in populations with elevated RHI exposure. If biomarkers are higher in current female athletes than in males at baseline, this could play a crucial role in later-life neurological health.

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN? Evidence-based sports injury prevention interventions for athletes often do not transition into routine practice within communities and require deliberate dissemination and implementation (D&I) strategies to bridge the gap and ensure accessibility. Female/woman/girl athletes have unique injury profiles and sporting environments that may require tailored strategies to deliver injury prevention interventions. WHAT ARE THE NEW FINDINGS? Adoption and cumulative use, the most reported D&I outcomes, were generally moderate to high. Positive perceptions, attitudes, intentions, and self-efficacy among athletes and coaches, prior injury experience and higher competition levels were facilitators of D&I in injury prevention programmes for female/woman/girl athletes. Many studies acknowledged health, performance, and environmental factors that could influence female/women/girls’ capability, opportunity and/or motivation to access, participate in, and benefit from evidence-based injury prevention interventions. For female/woman/girl athletes, interventions that are adaptable, sport-specific, engaging, and supported by education and/or workshops and/or policies are most likely to be used. In-person or online pre-season education followed by routine supervision in-season is resource-intensive and may improve implementation; however, further D&I focused studies are required. The whole sport system (eg, athletes, parents, coaches, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals, trainers and sport administrators) is critical to enhance implementation and sustainability of injury prevention interventions. Introduction Sport injury profiles and rates often differ by sex/gender, and injury outcomes (eg, return to sport and ongoing symptoms) are often worse in female, woman and/or girl (female/women/girl) athletes. Biological differences may partly drive these disparities, so too the interaction of sex/gender and sport context. Female/woman/girl athletes may have different training histories, sport exposure or facilitators and barriers to participation than male/man/boy athletes, ultimately influencing their injury risk. The extent to which injury prevention strategies are implemented with female/woman/girl athletes by athletes, coaches and organisations outside of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is unclear. Tailoring strategies to female/woman/girl athletes based on injury profile and sport context may be the key to preventing more injuries. Evidence-based interventions often do not inform routine practice in the communities they are meant to benefit, requiring deliberate strategies to expedite the process. Dissemination is the ‘active approach of spreading evidence-based interventions to the target audience via determined channels using planned strategies.’ Implementation encompasses ‘strategies and factors that support the initial integration and use of evidence-based interventions within a specific context’ and sustained use over time. Understanding what effective dissemination and implementation (D&I) strategies exist and factors associated with intervention use across socio-ecological levels will guide practice for athletes, support personnel (eg, coaches and health professionals) and organisations. This scoping review aimed to synthesise evidence related to D&I of injury prevention interventions to inform practical and research recommendations, as part of the Female, Woman and Girl Athlete Injury Prevention (FAIR) Consensus. Five other FAIR Consensus systematic reviews examined the efficacy and/or effectiveness of injury prevention interventions for lower-extremity, upper extremity, spine/trunk/pelvis and concussion injuries in female/woman/girl athletes. In this scoping review, we (1) describe how D&I of injury prevention interventions were measured, (2) examine the level of D&I and factors associated with D&I at multiple socio-ecological levels and (3) explore available D&I strategies. Methods The protocol was based on the Johanna Briggs Institute scoping review best practice guidelines and was registered prospectively on 23 July 2023 ( https://osf.io/eskz7/ ). Reporting was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) extension for Scoping Reviews Checklist ( ). Protocol deviations The protocol was updated (June 2024) to include papers with ≥25% female/woman/girl athletes (previously ≥1 athlete) to better represent the environment for this population. Further, papers only had to include a D&I outcome (protocol stated had to also report factors associated with D&I outcomes; ). Box 1 Equity, diversity and inclusion statement Female, woman and girl: In this review, we refer to the participants as ‘female, woman, and/or girl’ athletes (shortened into female/woman/girl) and ‘male, man, and/or boy’ athletes (male/man/boy). We recognise that these terms are not synonymous and may mean different things to different people. We also use the term ‘gender and/or sex’ (gender/sex). We acknowledge the active conversation on the meaning and definitions of gender and sex and note that the term ‘female(s)’ is not intended to reduce humans to their biological sex, and terms ‘women’ and ‘girls’ are not intended to reduce humans to their gender. Review planning and design: The FAIR Consensus Steering Committee planned and designed this review. This group (n=24, 80% women; n=17, 71% affiliated with IOC Research Centres for the prevention of injury and protection of athlete health) includes academics and sports medicine/health professionals (n=19; 79%) with broad expertise, such as epidemiology (n=18; 75%), injury prevention (n=21; 88%), sport sciences (n=4; 17%), health promotion (n=2; 8%) and career stage (n=7, late career; n=9, mid-career; n=8, early career) from four continents, who are mostly white, and from well-resourced countries. This group (n=24, 80% women; n=17, 71% affiliated with IOC Research Centres for the prevention of injury and protection of athlete health) includes academics and sports medicine/health professionals (n=19; 79%) with broad expertise, such as epidemiology (n=18; 75%), injury prevention (n=21; 88%), sport sciences (n=4; 17%), health promotion (n=2; 8%) and career stage (n=7, late career; n=9, mid-career; n=8, early career) from four continents, who are mostly white, and from well-resourced countries. Authors: for this scoping review were chosen by the FAIR Steering Committee based on relevant and diverse experiences, backgrounds, expertise and professions. This research team (n=29, 76% women) consists of early (49%), mid-career (34%) and senior (17%) researchers from physiotherapy, sport and exercise science, nursing, coaching, public health and data science disciplines. Authors are mostly white (83%), with 7% black (African)/African American (n=2), and 10% Asian (n=3). Authors spanned five continents (current residence) with 14% from countries with middle- to low-income birth rates. Authors self-reported lived experience as an athlete (n=13; 45%), coach (n=12; 41%), referee (n=1; 3%), health, medical or exercise practitioner (n=21; 72%) and member of sport organisation (n=12; 41%), government (n=3; 10%) or healthcare committees (n=4; 14%), covering paediatric (n=25; 86%), adult (n= 25; 86%) and Para sport (n=14; 48%) settings. Study participants: These included athletes (49% female/woman/girl), coaches, parents, teachers, athletic trainers, health and exercise professionals and local, national and international sport system administrators. Studies were conducted in 31 countries, across 81 sports. The effects of sociodemographic factors, including sex/gender, were explored. Patient and public involvement The FAIR Consensus External Advisory Committee (EAC) consists of eight women with lived experiences as athletes, team physicians/physiotherapists, coaches, sport scientists and leadership in sport, government, industry and/or healthcare organisations. The EAC provided feedback on this review (eg, eligible sports/populations, interpretation and practical implications) and will contribute to knowledge translation activities. EAC activities are further detailed in the methods of the FAIR consensus statement paper. Eligibility Population . The population of interest included female/woman/girl athletes of any age who were participating in sports competition and/or performance (ie, dance/performing arts) at any level (professional, amateur, grassroots and Para sports). Recreational activity (eg, running/skiing without competition) and active transportation (eg, cycling to work) were excluded. Given the underrepresentation of female/woman/girl athletes in sports medicine research, papers on mixed sex and gender were included, where≥25% were female/woman/girl athletes or individuals (eg, coaches and trainers) who worked with ≥25% of female/woman/girl athletes. The 25% cut-off aimed to increase the likelihood that the D&I strategies considered female/woman/girl athletes. Outcomes : Any D&I outcomes associated with a primary sports injury prevention intervention (eg, musculoskeletal, concussion, central/peripheral nervous system, eye and dental) were included. We considered all D&I terms (eg, awareness, adoption and exercise fidelity) and known implementation and socio-behavioural models/frameworks. Outcomes related to general injury knowledge without explicitly addressing prevention (eg, concussion symptom recognition) were excluded. Intervention: All injury prevention interventions/behaviours were eligible. Secondary prevention interventions were considered if the primary objective was to reduce the risk of subsequent injury. Interventions solely targeting injury risk factors (eg, strength and biomechanics) were excluded. Exposures (Aim 2). Papers evaluating factors associated with D&I of an injury prevention intervention were identified using a combination of D&I determinant models. Factors could be related to any level of the socio-ecological model: individual (eg, athlete injury experience and beliefs) interpersonal (eg, coach gender, relationships with teammates and parent beliefs), sport–system and community (eg, local, national, regional or international sporting body or government mandates/guidelines) or society (eg, public opinion/norms). Factors could also relate to intervention (eg, intervention duration and delivery method) or sociodemographic factors (eg, region and socioeconomic status). Study design . All primary research designs were included, from peer-reviewed journals or thesis/dissertation chapters. Review articles, protocols, conference abstracts and editorials/commentaries were excluded. Information sources An expert evidence synthesis health sciences librarian (KAH) developed and executed the search strategy according to the Cochrane Handbook and PERSiST guidance (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and Sports science), in consultation with authors KC, CE, CM, OO, BP and EV ( ). The search consisted of three main concepts: sports, prevention (both adapted from the sixth Consensus on Concussion in Sports) and dissemination/implementation. Nine databases were searched from 1996 to 2023 (Medline-OVID, CINAHL-EBSCOhost, APA PsycINFO-OVID, Cochrane Systematic Review Database-OVID, CENTRAL-OVID, SPORTDiscus-EBSCOhost, EMBASE-OVID and ERIC-EBSCOhost). ProQuest Dissertation & Theses Global was searched for dissertation/theses. Databases were searched on 14 December 2023, except CENTRAL and Cochrane Systematic Review Database (19 December 2023). Records were exported to Covidence (Version 2, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for deduplication and screening. Citation tracking (ie, 13 reviews related to D&I injury prevention interventions were excluded but tagged for later review) identified additional records, which went through the same screening process

ProQuest Dissertation & Theses Global was searched for dissertation/theses. Databases were searched on 14 December 2023, except CENTRAL and Cochrane Systematic Review Database (19 December 2023). Records were exported to Covidence (Version 2, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for deduplication and screening. Citation tracking (ie, 13 reviews related to D&I injury prevention interventions were excluded but tagged for later review) identified additional records, which went through the same screening process using Endnote and Excel. Selection of sources A rapid screen by eight reviewers excluded irrelevant (not related to sports) records and animal research. Inter-rater agreement was then established among all reviewers on a sample set of 50 records, with a minimum threshold of 80%. Reviewers not meeting this threshold screened another 50 records, continuing until ≥80% agreement was achieved. Twenty-four reviewers working in blinded pairs then screened titles/abstracts and full texts. Disagreements within pairs during screening and data extraction were resolved by consensus or discussion with a third reviewer. Quality assessment The Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018 was used to assess methodological quality across different study designs (quantitative RCTs, quantitative non-randomised trials, quantitative descriptive, qualitative and mixed methods). The MMAT was amended to remove the adherence/compliance criterion (as this was an inclusion criterion for the review). Scores were presented using a percentage descriptor, from 0 (no criteria met) to 100% (all criteria met). Based on the total score, individual papers were classified as high (≥75%), moderate (26%–74%) or low (≤25%) quality ( ). Data charting and appraisal A data extraction spreadsheet and instructions were developed and updated iteratively (by BP, CM and OO; ) during data extraction on a subset of eight papers. Following training (by BP, CM and OO), 24 authors in blinded pairs concurrently extracted data, including study characteristics (eg, design, year and country), participant details (eg, sport, role, age and competition level), intervention details (eg, type and duration), D&I outcomes (eg, 80% aware of mouthguards), D&I exposure variables (eg, delivery method and sport setting) and MMAT scores. Data extracted from qualitative papers were themes and exemplar quotes related to D&I outcomes and/or exposure variables of interest. Synthesis By population . Papers (n, %) were categorised according to participant type/s (by socio-ecological levels), sport/s represented, competition level/s, athlete age-group/s and injury prevention intervention type ( ). Box 2 Definitions of participant and intervention type, competition level, age-group Intervention types Training strategies: any exercise or training-based interventions specifically designed to prevent injury such as neuromuscular warm-up programmes and can include load monitoring/management programming, training design or coaching. Personal protective equipment: can include, but is not limited to helmets, mouthguards, protective eyewear, ankle/knee braces, breast protection and/or soft padded headgear. Policies, rules or laws: policies/rules/laws designed to prevent injury such as eliminating body checking, limiting contact practice and mandating mouthguard use. Other strategies include psychological intervention (eg , coping skills and motivational interviewing), education on multimodal strategies (eg, online concussion prevention education about equipment and coaching and contact training load), general injury prevention intervention not specified (eg, perceptions of injury prevention) No intervention (eg, perceived preventability of injuries and injury risk) Competition level Amateur: recreational, community-level, not defined as elite/elite sub-elite, or participating in local/regional competition. Sub-elite: defined as sub-elite by the study or participating in semi-professional competition. Elite: professional or elite as defined by the study or participating in national or international competition. Athlete age group Adults: aged >18 years (no upper limit on age) Paediatric = aged ≤18 years (no lower limit on age); paper includes children (aged <10) or adolescents (aged 10 to ≤18) By D&I approach: papers were identified as partially (hybrid type 1/2/3) or fully D&I-focussed ( ). A hybrid paper reported both clinical (eg, injury incidence) and D&I research outcomes. Box 3 Definitions of D&I outcomes according to the Quality Enhancement Research initiative (QUERI) Implementation Roadmap and study approach type. Implementation phase The QUERI Implementation Roadmap is a process and determinants model to guide translation of evidence-based interventions into practice. A paper could measure D&I outcomes in any phase. Pre-implementation Outcomes related to planning and dissemination of injury prevention D&I outcome categories: awareness, knowledge, expectations, perceptions (perceived injury risk, preventability, benefits, importance and norms), self-efficacy (belief in one’s ability to implement), intentions or barriers/facilitators/strategies related to dissemination. Implementation Outcomes related to implementation and delivery of injury prevention intervention. D&I outcome categories: feasibility, acceptability, adoption, cumulative utilisation, utilisation frequency, utilisation fidelity, exercise fidelity, duration fidelity, other implementation or delivery outcomes (eg, who delivers and timing of delivery) or barriers/facilitators/strategies related to implementation/delivery. Sustainment Outcomes related to sustainability and maintenance of injury prevention interventions. D&I outcome categories: reach, maintenance/long-term use, integration of policies/rules/laws, barriers/facilitators/strategies related to sustainment. Study approach Any study design could be included – randomised or non-randomised trials, and any observational quantitative or qualitative, or mixed methods designs. Individual papers were classified according to a “hierarchy of relevance” in relation to D&I objectives: observational-implementation (representing either hybrid/full) hybrid-experimental type 1 (D&I objective is secondary or exploratory) hybrid-experimental type 2 (D&I objective is of equal weight as clinical objective) hybrid-experimental type 3 (D&I objective is prioritised) full D&I experimental papers (D&I objective only) Hybrid effectiveness-implementation experimental studies could include randomised controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies or pre-experimental studies. Type 2 or 3 hybrid and full D&I studies were recognised as relevant for the D&I of evidence-based sports injury prevention. By outcomes . The lead authors (BP, OO, CM, KC and CE) developed a taxonomy of D&I outcome categories ( ) informed by implementation and socio-behavioural models/frameworks. Quantitative and qualitative outcomes could be reported by the users (eg, coaches and players), study personnel (eg, field observations) or other methods (eg, video). Phrases and definitions used by authors (eg, ‘median 12/13 exercises completed each session’) were mapped to the D&I outcome categories (eg, mapped to ‘utilisation fidelity’). Each D&I outcome category was then mapped to the pre-implementation, implementation or sustainment phase of the Quality Enhancement Research Initiative Implementation Roadmap ( ). The number of quantitative papers contributing data in each D&I outcome category and phase was reported. By exposure variables . Any factor associated with any D&I outcome was classified in five categories: socio-demographic, individual, interpersonal, sport system and community, and the number of papers with a quantitative estimate of the effect of the exposure variable was reported. Intervention factors (eg, type, duration and D&I strategy characteristics) were reported narratively. Quantitative and qualitative data were mapped to the same D&I outcomes and/or exposure framework ( ; example extraction is shown in ) and considered alongside quantitative data. Considering the synthesised findings, two authors (CM and BP) determined the presence of qualitative data that can enrich or oppose the quantitative data, and exemplar quotes were chosen to represent the qualitative data. Results Study characteristics The database searches identified 22 663 unique records. Following a rapid review, 10 298 titles and abstracts were screened, 1504 full-texts reviewed and 219 were eligible ( ). Citation searching identified 2615 additional citations, resulting in one paper. 220 papers were retained for synthesis (full list and characteristics in ). Studies were conducted in 32 countries, with nearly two-thirds (n=134) from the United States (n=63), Sweden (n=29), Australia (n=23) and Canada (n=19). Less than 10% of studies were conducted in Asia (n=18), Africa (n=4) and South America (n=1) ( ). Ten papers were theses/dissertations. Most papers were rated as having high (n=121/220) or moderate (n=74/220) quality ( ). Participants : 419 494 participants spanning 81 sports contributed to D&I outcome data. There were 96 790 athletes (49% female/women/girls). Representation decreased through the outer levels of the socio-ecological model, with few papers (12/220) including local, national or international sport system participants ( ). One in four papers studied only female/women/girl athletes ( ). Sports . Papers predominantly included team-based sports. The top five sports were football/soccer (n=81), basketball (n=53), volleyball (n=31), athletics (n=21) and handball (n=20). 11 Para sports were represented across two papers. Competition-level and age group . Papers included amateur (n=175), sub-elite (n=10), elite (n=63) and Para sport (n=2) athletes. Adult and paediatric athletes were represented in 124 and 144 papers, respectively (paediatric (aged 10 to ≤18), n=21 papers in children (aged <10), n=123 in adolescents). Intervention type . Papers evaluated D&I outcomes related to training interventions (n=113/220), PPE (n=41/220), policies/rules/laws (n=5/220) or other interventions (n=61/220, eg, counselling, multimodal education about training, injury management and general health; and . They explored earlier stages of intervention development such as athlete monitoring, risk factors and possible prevention strategies. Athletes and coaches highlighted a desire to be recognised: “ Para sport is sometimes not seen as elite sport, people don’t understand that we train as much as able-bodied elite athletes .” Dissemination and implementation outcomes: implementation roadmap The number of papers reporting quantitative D&I outcomes in pre-implementation, implementation and sustainment phases is shown in . The implementation phase was most represented (n=169, >350 outcomes), whereas the sustainment phase was least represented (n=26, <50 outcomes). Pre-implementation phase Of the 90 papers, 80 had observational-implementation (typically cross-sectional survey) designs. Most (61/90) evaluated athlete/coach perceptions about injury risk, preventability and prevention benefits ( ). Perceptions and attitudes were generally positive. For example, 10/15 papers reported that ≥80% of athletes/coaches perceive injuries to be preventable, and 20/38 papers reported that 50%–90% of athletes/coaches believed that training interventions (eg, exercise and load management) could reduce lower-limb injury risk, and mouthguards could prevent orofacial injuries. 50% to 95% of participants agreed that mouthguards could prevent orofacial injuries. There was agreement about the benefits of PPE to prevent concussion. Coach and athlete confidence to implement was less examined (9/90) and less positive (compared with their perceptions about intervention benefits). Awareness (30/90 papers) of lower-limb injury prevention programmes was moderate (11/30>60% athletes/coaches aware) to high (11/30>80% athletes/coaches aware) but awareness of sport- or organisation-specific programmes (eg, Knakontroll, 11+ and Activate Gaelic) was lower (25%–58%). Of the few papers in low- and middle-income countries, awareness, attitudes and adoption of training interventions and PPE was low (eg, 17%–25% were aware). Qualitative data (15/90) exploring pre-implementation D&I outcomes mostly supported the positive perceptions and attitudes. However, there were some negative athlete/coach perceptions; for example, common themes included that injuries are an inevitable part of sport, and athletes have limited knowledge and struggle to retain information or do not perceive that they are at risk of injury. For females/women/girls, the need to ‘understand the why’ and have equal access to education from experts was emphasised. Implementation phase Most papers with implementation outcomes (n=169) were observational-implementation (104/169) or type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation (47/169) studies in the implementation phase. D&I outcomes were predominantly related to adoption (109/169), utilisation frequency (42/169) and cumulative utilisation (33/169). Fidelity D&I outcomes were less commonly reported ( ). Adoption (109 papers, 174 outcomes ). Across all intervention types, adoption rates were spread across high (35/174), medium (n=62/174) and low (n=57/174) categories. In general, PPE had higher adoption rates (51% in high category) than training interventions (30% in high category). Qualitative data suggest that the high rates of PPE adoption may be due to it becoming a ‘habit’ and a ‘part of the uniform’. Cumulative utilisation (33 papers, 42 outcomes) and utilisation frequency (42 papers, 53 outcomes ). Cumulative utilisation was most commonly (29/42) defined as a proportion (%) of completed training intervention sessions, and was mostly medium (19/39) to high (20/39). For the utilisation frequency outcomes, most were medium (ie, 1–2 times per week, 30/53), with few in the high category (more than two times per week: 11/53). Fidelity outcomes . Utilisation fidelity (17/169) and exercise fidelity (20/169) were mostly sub-optimal; only 2/17 papers reported that most (>80%) programme elements were completed, and 2/20 reported that exercises were completed as prescribed (ie, no modifications). Poor acceptability of training interventions (eg, warm-up components) and consequent modifications may contribute to sub-optimal fidelity based on qualitative data. Sustainment phase Most papers in the sustainment phase (20/26) had observational-implementation designs, and most outcomes were related to intended maintenance (15/26) ( ). Most (>80%) athletes/coaches reported that they were likely to use the intervention in the future. Two papers measured maintenance (eg, 10% decrease in use at 3 years by clinical trial coaches). Evaluation of injury prevention policies at club/league/district level was limited (9/26), and the presence of policy was low (10%–25%). Reports of routine injury prevention education/workshops by local or national sporting or government were rare and mostly limited to football (eg, FIFA, >5000 coaches from 40 countries, Swedish football district workshops). Reports of routine injury prevention education/workshops by local or national sporting or government were rare and mostly limited to football (eg, FIFA, >5000 coaches from 40 countries, Swedish football district workshops). Online concussion education courses for athletes, parents, athletic trainers, teachers and coaches/club personnel have reached large audiences (eg, ‘Heads Up’ by United States Centres for Disease Control and Prevention and >600K course completions in the first 3 years). The initiatives shaped school policies (eg, compulsory completion of ‘Heads Up’) and cultural change: “ just a lot more about prevention and speaking to athletes about it (things like rebounding technique) to avoid concussions. In the past, I guess we were aware of them… but we weren’t super proactive about preventing them ” (teacher/coach) . Factors associated with dissemination and implementation outcomes 143 papers evaluated factors associated with D&I outcomes (113 quantitative papers, 24 qualitative and 12 mixed methods) (143 papers; ). Individual and interpersonal facilitators of D&I were athletes with an injury history, higher competition level and sport experience, and positive athlete/coach perceptions, attitudes, intentions and self-efficacy. The effect of athlete sex/gender was unclear. No other sociodemographic factors were clear barriers or facilitators of D&I. The number of papers evaluating each factor is listed in . Qualitative data were able to expand on other interpersonal (i), sport system (ii and iii) and societal factors (iv) such as the following: Interpersonal factors: modelling, early introduction: “It was ‘wow, they do it’. So, you see that the more senior players actually do it” (handball coach, male) 56 and “you get buy-in through developing habit and routine , so getting the girls into injury prevention at an early age is key” (player, Gaelic football). 73 Club resources, culture and attitudes: “Do you know, frustratingly, more than likely the men come first…. Yearly requests for improved medical support were ‘falling on deaf ears… One day we were waiting 45 min so obviously our warm-up had to be changed…” (women’s elite-level soccer player). 74 Club duty of care and the role of local experts: “There’s responsibility on the clubs… to keep players safe and make sure they are prepared in terms of warm-ups….have someone assigned the role of facilitator for injury prevention…be tuned into injury prevention and have an awareness. Ideally, facilitators would have healthcare backgrounds or link in with athletic therapists/physios” (coach, Gaelic football). 63 Influence of media on risk perception and awareness: “Television regarding sports concussions focused on the risks of participation in contact sports, causing parents to worry about their children participating in contact sports . In contrast, some coaches noted that discussion on social media has “helped take the taboo off of it” and made people more comfortable to talk about it” (college sport coach). Intervention characteristics: type of exercises (six papers) Six papers evaluated the effect of different types of training interventions on D&I outcomes. Conventional stretching/jogging warm-ups had equivalent D&I to a neuromuscular warm-up programme, whereas the 11+had better D&I outcomes compared with a novel warm-up (eg, a more time-conscious and adaptable programme). Intervention characteristics: acceptability (37 papers) The most reported barriers for training interventions were time (intervention length and competing priorities), lack of perceived relevance/sport-specificity or coach-reported lack of skills/knowledge or education/support/staff to implement (19 papers). Willingness to implement may decrease if the programme is >15 min (94% willing if 15 min, 56% for 20 min and 21% for 30 min). The top facilitators of training interventions were adaptability and ability for progressions/tailoring, sport-specificity, enjoyable, competitive and/partner-based exercises (19 papers). The top reported barriers for PPE were side effects (difficulty breathing/speaking and negative performance effects, 18 papers) and discomfort (15 papers). Dissemination and implementation strategy characteristics (67 experimental papers) Of the 67 experimental papers, 38 were RCTs, 16 had quasi-experimental and 14 had pre-experimental designs. Most (45/67) were hybrid type 1 that compared the effect of injury prevention intervention on standard practice/usual care. The remaining 22/67 had hybrid-experimental type 2 (n=7), hybrid-experimental type 3 (n=4) or full D&I experimental designs (n=11). What dissemination and implementation strategies? Education and/or workshops were delivered in person (41/67) or via online education materials (23/67). In-person delivery included physical demonstrations and/or practice and education (30/41), or education alone (11/41). Education and/or workshops can improve D&I outcomes (10/11 papers that measured D&I outcomes pre-post interventions), mostly in the pre-implementation phase (eg, knowledge, perceptions and confidence). Of the six papers comparing different D&I strategies, an in-person was superior to online materials, an animated video was superior to a scientific article and mobile apps were equivalent to online pamphlets.
