Who should deliver? When? Education and/or workshops were mostly delivered by study personnel (42/67), followed by health/exercise/medical professionals (9/67) or coaches (4/67) trained by the research team. When the timing of delivery was reported (41/67), it was mostly (29/41) delivered during pre-season. Who to target? Education and/or workshops targeted exclusively at athletes (29/67), coaches (20/67) or both (15/67). There were varying opinions on who was responsible for implementation. Many coaches believed players and/or role models were responsible and critical to buy-in : “Kids will be more likely to follow the role model player than follow the coach that’s harping on at them every day of the week” . Players often reported that coach motivation was critical, and “It would be virtually impossible (to do the injury prevention initiatives) without coach buy-in ”. Parents could play a critical role, particularly for concussion prevention strategies that rely on parents to purchase PPE. Parents’ education level, experiences (eg, contact sport or injury history) and attitudes may influence PPE adoption. Greater team resources and access to health/exercise/medical professionals may enhance D&I outcomes. However, the cost of accessing professionals and/or perceptions (eg, physiotherapist’s role is post-injury rehabilitation) may be barriers. A shared responsibility that fosters athlete, parent, coach, team, health and sport system leadership and culture appears critical. How are dissemination and implementation outcomes measured? D&I outcomes were mostly (55/67) reported in intervention groups only, mostly by athletes (33/67) or coaches/team personnel (23/67). Seven papers validated the coach/trainer D&I outcomes with field observations, and agreement ranged from 60% to 100%. Repeated measures were every session/2–3 time per week (22/67) or weekly (22/67), whereas cross-sectional assessments were typically at the end of the season (13/67). How much supervision and support? (56 experimental papers on training interventions) Most training interventions were incorporated into team practice (44/56), whereas 12/56 had a home/independent programme. Sixteen papers reported implementation supervision by study personnel (n=4 every session, n=6 weekly, n=2 periodic throughout season) or team trainers/health professionals (n=4, every session). Of the three papers evaluating the effect of supervision, all had better D&I outcomes than no supervision; however, only one was statistically significant. Nineteen papers included in-person or online/phone support delivered by study personnel to assist implementation (eg, troubleshoot and provide motivation). The effect of support on D&I outcomes was not evaluated. Discussion This scoping review synthesised the state of quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform current and future research and practice for the D&I of evidence-based injury prevention interventions for female/woman/girl athletes. The 220 included papers involved>4 00 000 participants, across multiple socio-ecological levels and 81 sports, and 49% were female/woman/girl athletes. The under-represented regions (Asia, Africa and South America), populations (eg, Para sport, sub-elite and children), D&I phases (sustainment), and study designs (D&I-focused trials) will direct future research on injury prevention D&I. Papers reported the level of D&I via >650 unique outcomes across the pre-implementation, implementation and sustainment phases, factors associated with D&I and current D&I strategies. Research targets: sociodemographic considerations The lack of research in Para sport, children, sub-elite and non-team sport athletes warrants future funding allocation and capacity building to better understand the unique implementation challenges in these settings. Understanding Para sport injury prevention needs is critical to inform intervention design and evaluation. Sociodemographic factors such as athlete and/or coach sex/gender or age, rurality, ethnic background, education level and school setting may influence implementation ( ) but require further research. Additional implementation barriers (eg, education access, funding opportunities and sports injury perceived importance relative to other health priorities) may exist in lower-income countries and/or more diverse cultural and religious contexts where gender norms, socioeconomic status, race and ethnicity intersect. Research targets: socio-ecological model outer layers, sustainment phase and dissemination and implementation trials Most participants were athletes (96,790) and coaches (277,923), highlighting limited research in parents, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals and sport system/school/government organisations. There is an opportunity for practitioners and sporting bodies and/or schools to disseminate information about evidence-based interventions, introduce policies and evaluate their implementation. Early introduction to prevention interventions in children may be important to form habits and change culture, facilitating implementation and sustainment at all ages, similar to school healthy eating initiatives. However, current sports injury prevention interventions are not evaluated in children and may not be relevant for younger players. were athletes (96,790) and coaches (277,923), highlighting limited research in parents, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals and sport system/school/government organisations. There is an opportunity for practitioners and sporting bodies and/or schools to disseminate information about evidence-based interventions, introduce policies and evaluate their implementation. Early introduction to prevention interventions in children may be important to form habits and change culture, facilitating implementation and sustainment at all ages, similar to school healthy eating initiatives. However, current sports injury prevention interventions are not evaluated in children and may not be relevant for younger players. Sustainment outcomes were rarely evaluated (26/220) – intentional research and practical efforts are critical to maintain injury prevention intervention use in female/woman/girl athletes. Co-producing strategies with sportsystem partners using implementation science frameworks may lead to more permanent integration of injury prevention interventions. Since few papers (22/220) used full D&I or hybrid effectiveness implementation type 2/3 designs, the most effective intervention/delivery characteristics (eg, type, education format/timing and level of supervision) remain unclear. Research targets: intervention type and dissemination and implementation outcomes The majority of papers were related to training interventions, and future research should explore the D&I of PPE and policy/rules/laws, which have been more extensively researched in male/men/boy’s contexts. Adoption was the most common D&I outcome assessed; however, it does not equate to how often or how well the intervention is used. More proximal D&I outcomes such as intervention adherence and its dimensions, including cumulative utilisation, utilisation frequency, utilisation fidelity and exercise fidelity, may facilitate dose–response analyses and inform essential programme components and potential adaptations. Practical targets: implementation strategies (who, what and how) Our practical recommendations are for female/women/girls, acknowledging data included mixed sex/gender studies (49% of athletes were female/woman/girl), and more targeted research is required. Fifty-five papers included only female/woman/girls ( ), and 36/165 mixed sex/gender papers disaggregated data ( ). Recommendations could be generalised to male/men/boys’ contexts, and potential female/women/girl-specific considerations are highlighted throughout. The positive perceptions and attitudes and moderate to high levels of adoption and cumulative utilisation identified in this review underpin our practical recommendations. Most D&I strategies included education and/or workshops either in-person (61%) or online (34%), typically delivered in pre-season (70%), by study personnel (63%), to athletes and/or coaches (96%). Few studies used deliverers beyond study personnel, and health/exercise/medical practitioners, coach/athlete educators, champions or technical directors should be involved in future implementation trials. Involving parents, team personnel and sport system administrators in education/workshops may share the responsibility, particularly in the context of under-resourced female/women/girls’ sport settings. Education usually includes lectures/information about injury risk, risk factors (often female sex-based), preventability and intervention efficacy. Given that injuries were perceived as a problem and preventative interventions beneficial, and several female-specific factors are non-modifiable (eg, anatomy), effort should shift to finding solutions to D&I barriers. Reduced lecturing style and more two-way discussions, self-practice, action planning and feedback with intervention users may enhance self-efficacy, adoption and sustained high-fidelity implementation. Pre-season education/workshops were mostly delivered in-person and may address the lack of transfer from better knowledge and positive intention to behaviour change. However, these strategies are resource-intensive, and only one of the two comparative RCTs reported superior D&I outcomes for a more supportive strategy. Although many RCTs had control groups with online materials, between-group D&I outcomes were rarely assessed, and few implementation cost-effectiveness studies exist, providing avenues for future research. In other fields (eg, psychiatry and nursing), online education minimised access and financial barriers with equivalent effectiveness (health/D&I outcomes) to in-person strategies. For PPE, online dissemination strategies may be sufficient, but the most effective platforms (eg, mobile apps, websites and social media) and formats (eg, video animations and infographics) remain unknown. Practical targets: implementation strategies (factors to consider) Practitioners may consider factors associated with D&I (previous injury experience, higher competition level and sport experience) to inform their strategies. Patient stories (ie, their injury experience and importance of prevention) could motivate others and optimise teammates, parents and support staff attitudes/intentions. Better D&I in higher competition levels may mean strategies are required to increase D&I in lower competition and less experienced athletes, for example, tailoring intervention content to amateur settings (eg, leaning into known facilitators for female/women/girls: fun, partner-based activities that are easy for coaches to learn and set up and adaptable to time/sport specific needs) and providing delivery support (eg, supervision and feedback). Debunking the perception that injury prevention is for the elite/more experienced/serious athlete and addressing the stigma about warming-up in social sport through education, and local champions/ambassadors/opinion leaders of all ages and abilities may be valuable. Female/women/girl athletes in lower competition levels may be more likely to engage in sport for social reasons; however, this should not disbar them from access to best practice injury prevention. Debunking the perception that injury prevention is for the elite/more experienced/serious athlete and addressing the stigma about warming-up in social sport through education, and local champions/ambassadors/opinion leaders of all ages and abilities may be valuable. Female/women/girl athletes in lower competition levels may be more likely to engage in sport for social reasons; however, this should not disbar them from access to best practice injury prevention. Sex-/gender-specific factors could be considered in intervention design and D&I strategies in some contexts. The effect of athlete sex/gender on D&I outcomes was unclear; however, it did influence D&I in 23/37 papers (in both directions, ). Gendered factors such as inequitable funding/support and expectations to conform to athletic ideals (eg, barrier to strength training) may affect D&I of interventions. Female-specific health factors (eg, breast tenderness and menstrual cycle/pelvic symptoms) may influence athlete participation (eg, reduced attendance or altered technique/performance in contact/impact activity due to symptoms). Raising coach awareness and providing strategies (eg, female health domain language they can use, environmental/personnel supports and technique/exercise modifications) that cater to needs specific to females/women/girls may enhance buy-in and uptake. However, some believe these approaches are unnecessarily progressive, and evaluation of sex/gender specific injury prevention interventions and D&I strategies is required. Practical targets: dissemination strategies Given that positive perceptions and attitudes among female/woman/girl athletes and coaches were associated with better D&I outcomes, pre-implementation initiatives to improve societal awareness and attitudes enhance implementation. Using social media campaigns to increase the uptake of evidence-based prevention interventions is effective (eg, immunology/vaccine uptake). Partnering with sporting organisations can help determine target markets, develop dissemination campaigns, while maintaining evidence-based messaging. Limitations This review only included publications in English, increasing the risk of language and publication bias. Sporting, education and government bodies may be employing injury prevention D&I initiatives without publishing their strategy or outcomes. The number of reviewers involved in screening and data extraction carries a small risk of error in data charting and interpretation. Under-representation of population groups (eg, Para sport, sub-elite and child athletes) limits the generalisability of findings. Conclusion This scoping review synthesised the state of quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform research and practice for the D&I of injury prevention interventions in female/woman/girl athletes. Perceptions and attitudes of coaches were mostly positive, whereas awareness, adoption and cumulative utilisation rates were moderate to high. Key facilitators of D&I include prior injury experience, higher competition level, greater sport experience and positive athlete and coach perceptions, attitudes, intentions and self-efficacy. Strategies to enhance D&I may include education and/or workshops in-person or online, delivered in pre-season by experts. There was limited attention on how well interventions are used or sustained and an unclear effect of supervision on D&I outcomes. Other critical gaps remain, and future research should prioritise under-represented regions (Asia, Africa and South America), populations (eg, studies on Para sport female/woman/girl only, sub-elite and children), D&I phases (sustainment) and study designs (D&I-focused trials). Most papers were focused on athletes and/or coaches. Engaging under-represented levels of the sport system (eg, parents, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals, trainers and sport/school administrators) may help address the lower rates and understanding of fidelity and long-term sustainability and ultimately reduce injury risk in female/woman/girl athletes. chunks.content: Introduction About 1.6 to 3.8 million sport-related concussions (SRCs) occur each year. ( ) Sport-related concussion is a subset of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) in which an athlete experiences a direct or indirect blow to the head, neck, or body, which results in temporary disturbance of brain functioning. ( ) Athletes who endure an SRC may experience alterations in one or more clinical domains such as cognition (e.g., attention, memory), vestibulo-ocular (e.g., imbalance, blurry vision), and a wide array of non-specific neurobehavioral symptoms (e.g., headache, fatigue, nausea, dizziness, mood changes). ( ) Heterogeneity in injury presentation creates challenges in the assessment and diagnosis ( ) as well as treatment ( ) of SRC. Heterogeneity in SRC presentation has resulted in preliminary investigations to identify distinct SRC profiles, which may provide understanding of the subtypes of SRC clinicians are most likely to encounter, establish their prevalence, and identify the profiles’ correlates to advance evidence-based personalized assessment and treatment. ( ) For example, Collins and colleagues proposed five symptom profiles of SRC: cognitive/fatigue, vestibular, posttraumatic migraine, anxiety/mood, and cervical. ( ) As the authors articulated, however, specific symptom profiles can be difficult to detect in the acute post-injury period, because of high comorbidity among symptoms soon after injury. This observation is supported by bifactor modeling analyses that found a single common factor to explain the vast majority (~95%) of the variance in acute SRC symptoms. ( , ) When these factor analytic results (which emphasize data at a sample/variable-level) are translating to individuals, they indicate that individuals with SRC vary much more in the overall burden of SRC symptoms than the type or profile of symptoms. Moreover, while previous research has identified initial symptom severity as the best predictor of symptom duration, ( ) a multimodal diagnostic approach including cognitive and balance domains is often recommended. Thus, efforts to identify distinct clinical profiles are likely to be more successful when looking across diverse, multimodal assessments as is routinely done in clinical practice through assessments of symptoms, cognitive performance, and balance. The objective of the current study was to use latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify distinct clinical profiles discernable from the main subscales of the SCAT (symptom severity, cognitive performance, balance performance) in the acute post-concussive phase. LPA is a data-driven, person-centered modeling method that seeks to parse a heterogeneous population into more homogenous subgroups (i.e., profiles), in order to identify groups of individuals that display different patterns of clinical presentation. More specifically, the approach involves modeling different numbers of latent (unobserved) profiles (for example, models with 2, 3, or 4 profiles), comparing the fit and interpretability of the models, and selecting a model that best balances consideration of fit (i.e., ability of the model to replicate the observed data) and interpretability. ( ) In contrast to variable-centered latent modeling approaches (e.g., factor modeling)—which seek to explain covariation among observed variables with underlying dimensions—LPA’s focus on identifying distinct profiles of individuals yields findings more closely tied to the pattern recognition that is inherent to clinical decision making. ( ) Therefore, using data from the large multicenter Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium, our specific aims were to: A) test the hypothesis that there are distinct clinical profiles discernable from acute post-injury scores on the SCAT symptom checklist, cognitive assessment (Standardized Assessment of Concussion [SAC], and balance assessment (Balance Error Scoring System [BESS]) and B) to examine the clinical utility of the identified profiles by characterizing their association with injury characteristics, neuropsychological outcomes, and clinical management-related outcomes. Methods Participants This secondary data analysis project combined data from two phases (1.0, 2.0) of the multicenter, prospective cohort studies run from 2014–2020 by the CARE Consortium. Details regarding data collection can be found in a prior publication. ( ) In brief, the initial sample comprised N= 5485 injured National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) athletes from 26 civilian colleges and 4 U.S. military service academies (flow diagram of included and excluded injuries can be found in the as ). Injuries were diagnosed by each sites’ athletic trainer. Participants were included if they completed the SCAT3/5 in 0–12 hours of injury with repeat injuries excluded, resulting in n = 1885 participants included in this analysis. IRB approval was obtained by each participating institution and all participants provided informed consent prior to participation in the study. Study design and measures The following clinical assessment measures were collected at both baseline, post-injury (0–12 hours; SCAT only), and 12–72 hours post-injury. Additionally, the study collected demographic information, injury characteristics (the presence of loss of consciousness [LOC] and/or posttraumatic amnesia [PTA]), and number of days it took for an athlete to return to full, unrestricted play (RTP) and return to asymptomatic (RTA). RTA was measured through patient report in interview of the day they felt they returned to their

Study design and measures The following clinical assessment measures were collected at both baseline, post-injury (0–12 hours; SCAT only), and 12–72 hours post-injury. Additionally, the study collected demographic information, injury characteristics (the presence of loss of consciousness [LOC] and/or posttraumatic amnesia [PTA]), and number of days it took for an athlete to return to full, unrestricted play (RTP) and return to asymptomatic (RTA). RTA was measured through patient report in interview of the day they felt they returned to their baseline symptom level. Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) Currently, the most widely used sideline assessment of SRC is the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT). The SCAT3/5 is a standardized tool used to measure a suspected concussion through quantifying multiple domains impacted by concussion such as symptom reporting (SCAT checklist), cognitive functioning (SAC), and balance (modified BESS). ( ) Of note, the most current (6 th ) edition of the SCAT retains the same version of the SCAT symptom checklist and BESS examined collected in the present study, while the SAC now requires a longer (10-item vs. 5-item) word list. As the present study evaluated profiles of standardized scores across symptom, cognitive, and balance domains, the findings are likely applicable across versions of the SCAT. The diagnostic utility of the SCAT5 is strong immediately post-injury and decreases significantly 3–5 days post-injury. ( ) The SCAT5 checklist comprises of 22 symptoms rated based on their current (post-injury) severity on a 7-point Likert scale (0= none, 6= severe). Total symptom severity scores range from 0–132. The SAC is a cognitive screening test measuring orientation, immediate memory, concentration, and delayed recall; scores range from 0–30 with 30 indicating a perfect score. ( , ) The modified BESS is a measure of postural stability that quantifies the number of balance errors examinees make while holding 3 positions on a firm surface. ( ) Modified BESS total scores range from 0–30, with higher scores reflecting more errors in maintaining postural stability. Brief Symptom Inventory 18 (BSI-18) The BSI-18 ( ) is a self-report measure of psychological distress and comprises a Global Severity Index (GSI) as well as three subscales (Anxiety, Depression, Somatization). Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = not at all, 4 = extremely) and summed into subscales (GSI range 0–72; subscale scores range from 0–24). We used the GSI as an outcome measure to capture differences in general emotional distress across profiles. Immediate Post-Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing (ImPACT) ImPACT ( ) is a computer-based assessment tool that is commonly used to assess athletes’ cognitive functioning before and after concussion. ImPACT measures the domains of verbal and visual memory (percent correct), motor speed and reaction time (average time), and impulse control. We used the verbal memory (VERM), visual memory (VISM), visual motor speed (VMS), and reaction time (RT) composites as outcome measures. Data Analysis We investigated demographic information, injury characteristics, and baseline functioning using IBM SPSS Version 27, Chicago, IL. ( ) All available cases were included in analysis regardless of site type (Division I-III college; military service academy); we examined the relationship between site type and latent profile membership to inform understanding of the applicability of the model across sites. We used Muthén & Muthén Mplus Version 8.9, Los Angeles, CA ( ) to conduct an LPA of SCAT5 symptom severity score, SAC total score, and BESS total score collected between 0–12 hours post-SRC as indicators. Each indicator was rescaled as z-scores, where higher values indicated worse performance/symptom severity, in order to transform the SCAT5 symptom checklist, SAC, and BESS onto the same scale. LPA handles missing data using a full information maximum likelihood (FIML) approach, which uses all available observed scores and is considered more robust than approaches that use listwise deletion. ( ) LPA is an exploratory approach in which the researchers derive the optimal number of profiles based on evidence from fit statistics and likelihood ratio tests, as well as consideration of subgroup size and clinical utility. We considered the following information criteria: Akaike’s Information Criterion [AIC; ( )], Bayesian Information Criterion [BIC; ( )], Sample-size Adjusted Bayesian Information Criterion [SABIC; ( )], and Consistent Akaike’s Information Criterion [CAIC; ( )]. Statistically, better model fit is reflected in lower AIC, BIC, SABIC, and CAIC values. We additionally considered the Adjusted Lo-Mendel-Rubin Test [LMR; ( )] and Bootstrapped Likelihood Ratio Test [BLRT; ( )]; a non-significant LMR demonstrates a more parsimonious model, whereas a significant BLRT indicates better fit than the previous K-1 model. Lastly, we included a measure of entropy, which measures separation between profiles (higher entropy indicates more separation). For more detailed information regarding the above mentioned information criteria and likelihood ratio tests see Ferguson, Moore,

We additionally considered the Adjusted Lo-Mendel-Rubin Test [LMR; ( )] and Bootstrapped Likelihood Ratio Test [BLRT; ( )]; a non-significant LMR demonstrates a more parsimonious model, whereas a significant BLRT indicates better fit than the previous K-1 model. Lastly, we included a measure of entropy, which measures separation between profiles (higher entropy indicates more separation). For more detailed information regarding the above mentioned information criteria and likelihood ratio tests see Ferguson, Moore, & Hull (2020). ( ) We investigated information criteria and likelihood ratio tests for up to 7 profiles, considering a combination of fit statistics and practice considerations (e.g., size and conceptual distinctions between groups) to determine the most optimal configuration. To investigate differences between latent profile group membership and categorical variables (e.g., sex, age, race, ethnicity, NCAA D1-III institution type, history of previous concussion, previous history of LD and/or ADHD, and LOC and/or PTA), we computed Chi-square tests of independence and Cramer’s V effect sizes (small effect = .07-.21, medium effect = .21-.35, and large effect = >.35). ( ) We used general linear models with the Sidak correction for post-hoc analyses to examine the association between profile group membership and continuously scaled baseline factors (e.g., sex, age, race, institution type, BSI-18 GSI, SCAT5 symptom severity, SAC total score, BESS total score) as well as 12–72 hour measures (e.g., BSI-18 GSI, SCAT5 symptom severity, SAC total score, BESS total score, and ImPACT VERM, VISM, VMS, and RT). Effect sizes reflected the association between latent profile group membership and continuous variables were calculated using partial eta squared (η p 2 ; small effect = .10-.25, medium effect = .25-.50, and large effect = > .50). ( ) Statistical significance was determined as p < .05. Models predicting outcomes from latent profile group membership were performed both as univariable models and multivariable models controlling for baseline differences and demographic factors that demonstrated significant differences (sex, race, ethnicity, and institution type) among latent profiles. Of note, age, history of concussion, and previous history of LD and/or ADHD did not demonstrate significant differences among latent profiles and therefore were not controlled for. Lastly, we examined the association between acute SCAT5 latent profile and time to symptom recovery and RTP using Kaplan Meier plots and logrank tests. Cox proportional hazards was considered but not used due to violations of critical assumptions. The overall association between latent profile and each outcome was determined through an overall logrank test, with post-hoc pairwise tests performed to compare the most resilient (Low Impairment) profile to the other profiles. Results Demographic and baseline information of the overall sample as well as each latent profile are presented in . Overall, the sample ranged in age from 17.3–26.7 years ( M [ SD ]= 20.0 [1.4]) and was 64% male and 66% white. Latent Profile Analysis Based on LPA fit statistics ( ) as well as practical considerations such as profile utility and size, a 6-profile model was selected. Zero-to-twelve-hour post-injury mean and standard deviations were used to calculate SCAT5 (M = 28.8, SD = 20.6), SAC (M = 26.2 SD = 3.0), and BESS (M = 17.6, SD = 8.7) z-scores. Profiles were labeled based on their mean z-scores on SCAT5 symptom severity, SAC score, and BESS score as Low Impairment (prevalence = 65.8%), High Cognitive Impairment (5.4%), High Balance Impairment (5.8%), High Symptom Severity (16.4%), Moderate Global Impairment (5.4%), and Severe Global Impairment (1.1%). Given the size of the Severe Global Impairment profile (n= 20) and conceptual similarity to the Moderate Global Impairment profile, the Severe Global Impairment and Moderate Global Impairment profiles were collapsed into an overall Global Impairment profile (n= 123) for the purpose of illustration in and analyses associating profile group membership and other variables. displays the mean SCAT5 scores and prevalence of the original 6-profile model. Therefore, five profiles were retained and mean z-scores scores are reported in : Low Impairment (mean SCAT5, SAC, and BESS z-score ranging from −0.51 to −0.29), High Cognitive Impairment (mean SAC z-score= 1.85), High Balance Impairment (mean BESS z-score= 1.96), High Symptom Severity (mean SCAT5 z-score= 1.27), and Global Impairment (mean SCAT5, SAC, and BESS z-scores ranging from 1.37 to 1.92). Most of the population fell into the Low Impairment range (65.8%), a reflection of the relatively subtle clinical impact of many SRCs. However, a meaningful number of participants experienced marked impairment on at least one SCAT5 subscore within 0–12 hours of injury (34.2%). Those that demonstrate impairment most commonly experience isolated high symptom severity (16.4%), followed by global impairments (6.5%) and isolated impairments in balance (5.8%) or cognition (5.4%). The variability in profile membership demonstrates the heterogeneity seen in symptoms/impairment post-SRC and supports the use of multidimensional tools in the acute post-injury period such as the SCAT3/5 or more recently published SCAT6. ( ) The identified profiles demonstrated unique associations across demographic and baseline factors. For example, there were more females in the High Symptom Severity profile whereas the High Balance profile was younger. Following previous research finding variable associations with demographic characteristics and subsequent SRC symptoms/impairments, ( , , ) we explored how demographic characteristics may be related to clinical profiles on the SCAT5. The association of demographic characteristics with the identified profiles allows clinicians to use the profiles instead of or in tandem with demographic variables to make informed decisions when assessing a patient and anticipating later outcomes. The identified profiles logically relate to baseline factors (e.g., High Balance Impairment group demonstrated more balance difficulties at baseline). Therefore, these findings may allow for clinicians and/or athletic trainers to anticipate how a concussion may impact an athlete prior to their injury based on their baseline performance. Moreover, given the association between baseline factors and SRC profiles, future research could investigate how, for example, balance training for athletes with baseline high balance impairment may impact their recovery should they sustain an SRC. Despite the significant association with baseline performance and identified profiles, the profiles appeared to independently predict outcomes when controlling for relevant baseline and demographic characteristics. The prevalence of LOC and/or PTA were most commonly found in the High Cognitive Impairment and Global Impairment profiles, suggesting that cognitive and global impairment may indicate higher incidence of acute injury characteristics in collegiate athletes. Furthermore, outcome analyses revealed that the identified profiles were logically and consistently associated with 12–72 hour SCAT5 (e.g., High Balance Impairment demonstrated more balance difficulties at 12–72 hours) and ImPACT outcomes (e.g., Low Impairment demonstrated better ImPACT scores across all subtests). This pattern allows clinicians to both anticipate symptomology/impairment based on SCAT5 profile membership as well as tailor treatment based on their patient’s acute profile membership. For example, given that the High Balance Impairment group continues to demonstrate balance impairment days post-injury, patients in this profile may benefit from vestibulo-ocular physical therapy to aid with their SRC recovery. ( ) Our findings on return to asymptomatic and play are consistent with previous research documenting that high symptom reporting is predictive of prolonged recovery from an SRC. ( , ) For example, the Global Impairment and High Symptom Severity groups demonstrated the longest periods of return to asymptomatic and play. Moreover, we found important prognostic information in groups without high symptom severity, with the High Balance Impairment groups demonstrating slower recovery than the Low Impairment group. However, the configuration of the profiles is not expected to change given the minimal changes between the main elements of the SCAT over time and our modeling of z-scores, which should reduce the impact of different score ranges in the SAC across versions of the SCAT. Lastly, while the current study focused on multimodal assessment, not all assessment modalities were used (e.g., vestibulo-ocular). Therefore, future research could expand upon this investigation by including other SRC measurement modalities. In conclusion, we found that college athletes and military service academy cadets display five qualitatively distinct profiles of symptoms, cognitive performance, and balance performance on the SCAT5 from 0–12 hours post-concussion. Acute SCAT5 profile is associated with baseline factors and is also independently associated with later clinical outcomes. The findings support the use of multimodal concussion assessments in the acute post-concussive period and provide clinically relevant data in the interpretation of SCAT5 profiles specifically. The identification and subsequent exploration of SRC profiles provides empirical evidence for clinicians to personalize treatment of a heterogenous injury. By considering the profile of performance across SCAT5 symptom, cognitive, and balance subscales, the findings validate the growing clinical movement of using personalized approaches to guide recommendations and treatment. chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN? Evidence-based sports injury prevention interventions for athletes often do not transition into routine practice within communities and require deliberate dissemination and implementation (D&I) strategies to bridge the gap and ensure accessibility. Female/woman/girl athletes have unique injury profiles and sporting environments that may require tailored strategies to deliver injury prevention interventions. WHAT ARE THE NEW FINDINGS? Adoption and cumulative use, the most reported D&I outcomes, were generally moderate to high. Positive perceptions, attitudes, intentions, and self-efficacy among athletes and coaches, prior injury experience and higher competition levels were facilitators of D&I in injury prevention programmes for female/woman/girl athletes. Many studies acknowledged health, performance, and environmental factors that could influence female/women/girls’ capability, opportunity and/or motivation to access, participate in, and benefit from evidence-based injury prevention interventions. For female/woman/girl athletes, interventions that are adaptable, sport-specific, engaging, and supported by education and/or workshops and/or policies are most likely to be used. In-person or online pre-season education followed by routine supervision in-season is resource-intensive and may improve implementation; however, further D&I focused studies are required. The whole sport system (eg, athletes, parents, coaches, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals, trainers and sport administrators) is critical to enhance implementation and sustainability of injury prevention interventions. Introduction Sport injury profiles and rates often differ by sex/gender, and injury outcomes (eg, return to sport and ongoing symptoms) are often worse in female, woman and/or girl (female/women/girl) athletes. Biological differences may partly drive these disparities, so too the interaction of sex/gender and sport context. Female/woman/girl athletes may have different training histories, sport exposure or facilitators and barriers to participation than male/man/boy athletes, ultimately influencing their injury risk. The extent to which injury prevention strategies are implemented with female/woman/girl athletes by athletes, coaches and organisations outside of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is unclear. Tailoring strategies to female/woman/girl athletes based on injury profile and sport context may be the key to preventing more injuries. Evidence-based interventions often do not inform routine practice in the communities they are meant to benefit, requiring deliberate strategies to expedite the process. Dissemination is the ‘active approach of spreading evidence-based interventions to the target audience via determined channels using planned strategies.’ Implementation encompasses ‘strategies and factors that support the initial integration and use of evidence-based interventions within a specific context’ and sustained use over time. Understanding what effective dissemination and implementation (D&I) strategies exist and factors associated with intervention use across socio-ecological levels will guide practice for athletes, support personnel (eg, coaches and health professionals) and organisations. This scoping review aimed to synthesise evidence related to D&I of injury prevention interventions to inform practical and research recommendations, as part of the Female, Woman and Girl Athlete Injury Prevention (FAIR) Consensus. Five other FAIR Consensus systematic reviews examined the efficacy and/or effectiveness of injury prevention interventions for lower-extremity, upper extremity, spine/trunk/pelvis and concussion injuries in female/woman/girl athletes. In this scoping review, we (1) describe how D&I of injury prevention interventions were measured, (2) examine the level of D&I and factors associated with D&I at multiple socio-ecological levels and (3) explore available D&I strategies. Methods The protocol was based on the Johanna Briggs Institute scoping review best practice guidelines and was registered prospectively on 23 July 2023 ( https://osf.io/eskz7/ ). Reporting was guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) extension for Scoping Reviews Checklist ( ). Protocol deviations The protocol was updated (June 2024) to include papers with ≥25% female/woman/girl athletes (previously ≥1 athlete) to better represent the environment for this population. Further, papers only had to include a D&I outcome (protocol stated had to also report factors associated with D&I outcomes; ). We recognise that these terms are not synonymous and may mean different things to different people. We also use the term ‘gender and/or sex’ (gender/sex). We acknowledge the active conversation on the meaning and definitions of gender and sex and note that the term ‘female(s)’ is not intended to reduce humans to their biological sex, and terms ‘women’ and ‘girls’ are not intended to reduce humans to their gender. Authors: for this scoping review were chosen by the FAIR Steering Committee based on relevant and diverse experiences, backgrounds, expertise and professions. This research team (n=29, 76% women) consists of early (49%), mid-career (34%) and senior (17%) researchers from physiotherapy, sport and exercise science, nursing, coaching, public health and data science disciplines. Authors are mostly white (83%), with 7% black (African)/African American (n=2), and 10% Asian (n=3). Authors spanned five continents (current residence) with 14% from countries with middle- to low-income birth rates. Authors self-reported lived experience as an athlete (n=13; 45%), coach (n=12; 41%), referee (n=1; 3%), health, medical or exercise practitioner (n=21; 72%) and member of sport organisation (n=12; 41%), government (n=3; 10%) or healthcare committees (n=4; 14%), covering paediatric (n=25; 86%), adult (n= 25; 86%) and Para sport (n=14; 48%) settings. Study participants: These included athletes (49% female/woman/girl), coaches, parents, teachers, athletic trainers, health and exercise professionals and local, national and international sport system administrators. Studies were conducted in 31 countries, across 81 sports. The effects of sociodemographic factors, including sex/gender, were explored. Patient and public involvement The FAIR Consensus External Advisory Committee (EAC) consists of eight women with lived experiences as athletes, team physicians/physiotherapists, coaches, sport scientists and leadership in sport, government, industry and/or healthcare organisations. The EAC provided feedback on this review (eg, eligible sports/populations, interpretation and practical implications) and will contribute to knowledge translation activities. EAC activities are further detailed in the methods of the FAIR consensus statement paper. Eligibility Population . The population of interest included female/woman/girl athletes of any age who were participating in sports competition and/or performance (ie, dance/performing arts) at any level (professional, amateur, grassroots and Para sports). Recreational activity (eg, running/skiing without competition) and active transportation (eg, cycling to work) were excluded. Given the underrepresentation of female/woman/girl athletes in sports medicine research, papers on mixed sex and gender were included, where≥25% were female/woman/girl athletes or individuals (eg, coaches and trainers) who worked with ≥25% of female/woman/girl athletes. The 25% cut-off aimed to increase the likelihood that the D&I strategies considered female/woman/girl athletes. Outcomes : Any D&I outcomes associated with a primary sports injury prevention intervention (eg, musculoskeletal, concussion, central/peripheral nervous system, eye and dental) were included. We considered all D&I terms (eg, awareness, adoption and exercise fidelity) and known implementation and socio-behavioural models/frameworks. Outcomes related to general injury knowledge without explicitly addressing prevention (eg, concussion symptom recognition) were excluded. Intervention: All injury prevention interventions/behaviours were eligible. Secondary prevention interventions were considered if the primary objective was to reduce the risk of subsequent injury. Interventions solely targeting injury risk factors (eg, strength and biomechanics) were excluded. Exposures (Aim 2). Papers evaluating factors associated with D&I of an injury prevention intervention were identified using a combination of D&I determinant models. Factors could be related to any level of the socio-ecological model: individual (eg, athlete injury experience and beliefs) interpersonal (eg, coach gender, relationships with teammates and parent beliefs), sport–system and community (eg, local, national, regional or international sporting body or government mandates/guidelines) or society (eg, public opinion/norms). Factors could also relate to intervention (eg, intervention duration and delivery method) or sociodemographic factors (eg, region and socioeconomic status). Study design . All primary research designs were included, from peer-reviewed journals or thesis/dissertation chapters. Review articles, protocols, conference abstracts and editorials/commentaries were excluded. Information sources An expert evidence synthesis health sciences librarian (KAH) developed and executed the search strategy according to the Cochrane Handbook and PERSiST guidance (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and Sports science), in consultation with authors KC, CE, CM, OO, BP and EV ( ). The search consisted of three main concepts: sports, prevention (both adapted from the sixth Consensus on Concussion in Sports) and dissemination/implementation. Nine databases were searched from 1996 to 2023 (Medline-OVID, CINAHL-EBSCOhost, APA PsycINFO-OVID, Cochrane Systematic Review Database-OVID, CENTRAL-OVID, SPORTDiscus-EBSCOhost, EMBASE-OVID and ERIC-EBSCOhost). ProQuest Dissertation & Theses Global was searched for dissertation/theses. Databases were searched on 14 December 2023, except CENTRAL and Cochrane Systematic Review Database (19 December 2023). Records were exported to Covidence (Version 2, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for deduplication and screening. Nine databases were searched from 1996 to 2023 (Medline-OVID, CINAHL-EBSCOhost, APA PsycINFO-OVID, Cochrane Systematic Review Database-OVID, CENTRAL-OVID, SPORTDiscus-EBSCOhost, EMBASE-OVID and ERIC-EBSCOhost). ProQuest Dissertation & Theses Global was searched for dissertation/theses. Databases were searched on 14 December 2023, except CENTRAL and Cochrane Systematic Review Database (19 December 2023). Records were exported to Covidence (Version 2, Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia) for deduplication and screening. Citation tracking (ie, 13 reviews related to D&I injury prevention interventions were excluded but tagged for later review) identified additional records, which went through the same screening process using Endnote and Excel. Selection of sources A rapid screen by eight reviewers excluded irrelevant (not related to sports) records and animal research. Inter-rater agreement was then established among all reviewers on a sample set of 50 records, with a minimum threshold of 80%. Reviewers not meeting this threshold screened another 50 records, continuing until ≥80% agreement was achieved. Twenty-four reviewers working in blinded pairs then screened titles/abstracts and full texts. Disagreements within pairs during screening and data extraction were resolved by consensus or discussion with a third reviewer. Quality assessment The Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018 was used to assess methodological quality across different study designs (quantitative RCTs, quantitative non-randomised trials, quantitative descriptive, qualitative and mixed methods). The MMAT was amended to remove the adherence/compliance criterion (as this was an inclusion criterion for the review). Scores were presented using a percentage descriptor, from 0 (no criteria met) to 100% (all criteria met). Based on the total score, individual papers were classified as high (≥75%), moderate (26%–74%) or low (≤25%) quality ( ). Data charting and appraisal A data extraction spreadsheet and instructions were developed and updated iteratively (by BP, CM and OO; ) during data extraction on a subset of eight papers. Following training (by BP, CM and OO), 24 authors in blinded pairs concurrently extracted data, including study characteristics (eg, design, year and country), participant details (eg, sport, role, age and competition level), intervention details (eg, type and duration), D&I outcomes (eg, 80% aware of mouthguards), D&I exposure variables (eg, delivery method and sport setting) and MMAT scores. Data extracted from qualitative papers were themes and exemplar quotes related to D&I outcomes and/or exposure variables of interest. Synthesis By population . Papers (n, %) were categorised according to participant type/s (by socio-ecological levels), sport/s represented, competition level/s, athlete age-group/s and injury prevention intervention type ( ). Box 2 Definitions of participant and intervention type, competition level, age-group Intervention types Training strategies: any exercise or training-based interventions specifically designed to prevent injury such as neuromuscular warm-up programmes and can include load monitoring/management programming, training design or coaching. Personal protective equipment: can include, but is not limited to helmets, mouthguards, protective eyewear, ankle/knee braces, breast protection and/or soft padded headgear. Policies, rules or laws: policies/rules/laws designed to prevent injury such as eliminating body checking, limiting contact practice and mandating mouthguard use. Other strategies include psychological intervention (eg , coping skills and motivational interviewing), education on multimodal strategies (eg, online concussion prevention education about equipment and coaching and contact training load), general injury prevention intervention not specified (eg, perceptions of injury prevention) No intervention (eg, perceived preventability of injuries and injury risk) Competition level Amateur: recreational, community-level, not defined as elite/elite sub-elite, or participating in local/regional competition. Sub-elite: defined as sub-elite by the study or participating in semi-professional competition. Elite: professional or elite as defined by the study or participating in national or international competition. Athlete age group Adults: aged >18 years (no upper limit on age) Paediatric = aged ≤18 years (no lower limit on age); paper includes children (aged <10) or adolescents (aged 10 to ≤18) By D&I approach: papers were identified as partially (hybrid type 1/2/3) or fully D&I-focussed ( ). A hybrid paper reported both clinical (eg, injury incidence) and D&I research outcomes. Box 3 Definitions of D&I outcomes according to the Quality Enhancement Research initiative (QUERI) Implementation Roadmap and study approach type. Implementation phase The QUERI Implementation Roadmap is a process and determinants model to guide translation of evidence-based interventions into practice. A paper could measure D&I outcomes in any phase. Pre-implementation Outcomes related to planning and dissemination of injury prevention D&I outcome categories: awareness, knowledge, expectations, perceptions (perceived injury risk, preventability, benefits, importance and norms), self-efficacy (belief in one’s ability to implement), intentions or barriers/facilitators/strategies related to dissemination. Implementation Outcomes related to implementation and delivery of injury prevention intervention. D&I outcome categories: feasibility, acceptability, adoption, cumulative utilisation, utilisation frequency, utilisation fidelity, exercise fidelity, duration fidelity, other implementation or delivery outcomes (eg, who delivers and timing of delivery) or barriers/facilitators/strategies related to implementation/delivery. For utilisation frequency: high (>2 times per week), medium (1–2 times per week), and low (<1 time per week) based on reported optimal adherence cut-offs. Sustainment Outcomes related to sustainability and maintenance of injury prevention interventions. D&I outcome categories: reach, maintenance/long-term use, integration of policies/rules/laws, barriers/facilitators/strategies related to sustainment. Study approach Any study design could be included – randomised or non-randomised trials, and any observational quantitative or qualitative, or mixed methods designs. Individual papers were classified according to a “hierarchy of relevance” in relation to D&I objectives: observational-implementation (representing either hybrid/full) hybrid-experimental type 1 (D&I objective is secondary or exploratory) hybrid-experimental type 2 (D&I objective is of equal weight as clinical objective) hybrid-experimental type 3 (D&I objective is prioritised) full D&I experimental papers (D&I objective only) Hybrid effectiveness-implementation experimental studies could include randomised controlled trials, quasi-experimental studies or pre-experimental studies. Type 2 or 3 hybrid and full D&I studies were recognised as relevant for the D&I of evidence-based sports injury prevention. By outcomes . The lead authors (BP, OO, CM, KC and CE) developed a taxonomy of D&I outcome categories ( ) informed by implementation and socio-behavioural models/frameworks. Quantitative and qualitative outcomes could be reported by the users (eg, coaches and players), study personnel (eg, field observations) or other methods (eg, video). Phrases and definitions used by authors (eg, ‘median 12/13 exercises completed each session’) were mapped to the D&I outcome categories (eg, mapped to ‘utilisation fidelity’). Each D&I outcome category was then mapped to the pre-implementation, implementation or sustainment phase of the Quality Enhancement Research Initiative Implementation Roadmap ( ). The number of quantitative papers contributing data in each D&I outcome category and phase was reported. By exposure variables . Any factor associated with any D&I outcome was classified in five categories: socio-demographic, individual, interpersonal, sport system and community, and the number of papers with a quantitative estimate of the effect of the exposure variable was reported. Intervention factors (eg, type, duration and D&I strategy characteristics) were reported narratively. Quantitative and qualitative data were mapped to the same D&I outcomes and/or exposure framework ( ; example extraction is shown in ) and considered alongside quantitative data. Considering the synthesised findings, two authors (CM and BP) determined the presence of qualitative data that can enrich or oppose the quantitative data, and exemplar quotes were chosen to represent the qualitative data. Results Study characteristics The database searches identified 22 663 unique records. Following a rapid review, 10 298 titles and abstracts were screened, 1504 full-texts reviewed and 219 were eligible ( ). Citation searching identified 2615 additional citations, resulting in one paper. 220 papers were retained for synthesis (full list and characteristics in ). Studies were conducted in 32 countries, with nearly two-thirds (n=134) from the United States (n=63), Sweden (n=29), Australia (n=23) and Canada (n=19). Less than 10% of studies were conducted in Asia (n=18), Africa (n=4) and South America (n=1) ( ). Ten papers were theses/dissertations. Most papers were rated as having high (n=121/220) or moderate (n=74/220) quality ( ). Participants : 419 494 participants spanning 81 sports contributed to D&I outcome data. There were 96 790 athletes (49% female/women/girls). Representation decreased through the outer levels of the socio-ecological model, with few papers (12/220) including local, national or international sport system participants ( ). Pre-implementation phase Of the 90 papers, 80 had observational-implementation (typically cross-sectional survey) designs. Most (61/90) evaluated athlete/coach perceptions about injury risk, preventability and prevention benefits ( ). Perceptions and attitudes were generally positive. For example, 10/15 papers reported that ≥80% of athletes/coaches perceive injuries to be preventable, and 20/38 papers reported that 50%–90% of athletes/coaches believed that training interventions (eg, exercise and load management) could reduce lower-limb injury risk, and mouthguards could prevent orofacial injuries. 50% to 95% of participants agreed that mouthguards could prevent orofacial injuries. There was agreement about the benefits of PPE to prevent concussion. Coach and athlete confidence to implement was less examined (9/90) and less positive (compared with their perceptions about intervention benefits). Awareness (30/90 papers) of lower-limb injury prevention programmes was moderate (11/30>60% athletes/coaches aware) to high (11/30>80% athletes/coaches aware) but awareness of sport- or organisation-specific programmes (eg, Knakontroll, 11+ and Activate Gaelic) was lower (25%–58%). Of the few papers in low- and middle-income countries, awareness, attitudes and adoption of training interventions and PPE was low (eg, 17%–25% were aware). Qualitative data (15/90) exploring pre-implementation D&I outcomes mostly supported the positive perceptions and attitudes. However, there were some negative athlete/coach perceptions; for example, common themes included that injuries are an inevitable part of sport, and athletes have limited knowledge and struggle to retain information or do not perceive that they are at risk of injury. For females/women/girls, the need to ‘understand the why’ and have equal access to education from experts was emphasised. Implementation phase Most papers with implementation outcomes (n=169) were observational-implementation (104/169) or type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation (47/169) studies in the implementation phase. D&I outcomes were predominantly related to adoption (109/169), utilisation frequency (42/169) and cumulative utilisation (33/169). Fidelity D&I outcomes were less commonly reported ( ). Adoption (109 papers, 174 outcomes ). Across all intervention types, adoption rates were spread across high (35/174), medium (n=62/174) and low (n=57/174) categories. In general, PPE had higher adoption rates (51% in high category) than training interventions (30% in high category). Qualitative data suggest that the high rates of PPE adoption may be due to it becoming a ‘habit’ and a ‘part of the uniform’. Cumulative utilisation (33 papers, 42 outcomes) and utilisation frequency (42 papers, 53 outcomes ). Cumulative utilisation was most commonly (29/42) defined as a proportion (%) of completed training intervention sessions, and was mostly medium (19/39) to high (20/39). For the utilisation frequency outcomes, most were medium (ie, 1–2 times per week, 30/53), with few in the high category (more than two times per week: 11/53). Fidelity outcomes . Utilisation fidelity (17/169) and exercise fidelity (20/169) were mostly sub-optimal; only 2/17 papers reported that most (>80%) programme elements were completed, and 2/20 reported that exercises were completed as prescribed (ie, no modifications). Poor acceptability of training interventions (eg, warm-up components) and consequent modifications may contribute to sub-optimal fidelity based on qualitative data. Intervention characteristics: type of exercises (six papers) Six papers evaluated the effect of different types of training interventions on D&I outcomes. Conventional stretching/jogging warm-ups had equivalent D&I to a neuromuscular warm-up programme, whereas the 11+had better D&I outcomes compared with a novel warm-up (eg, a more time-conscious and adaptable programme). Intervention characteristics: acceptability (37 papers) The most reported barriers for training interventions were time (intervention length and competing priorities), lack of perceived relevance/sport-specificity or coach-reported lack of skills/knowledge or education/support/staff to implement (19 papers). Willingness to implement may decrease if the programme is >15 min (94% willing if 15 min, 56% for 20 min and 21% for 30 min). The top facilitators of training interventions were adaptability and ability for progressions/tailoring, sport-specificity, enjoyable, competitive and/partner-based exercises (19 papers). The top reported barriers for PPE were side effects (difficulty breathing/speaking and negative performance effects, 18 papers) and discomfort (15 papers). Most (45/67) were hybrid type 1 that compared the effect of injury prevention intervention on standard practice/usual care. Education and/or workshops targeted exclusively at athletes (29/67), coaches (20/67) or both (15/67). There were varying opinions on who was responsible for implementation. Many coaches believed players and/or role models were responsible and critical to buy-in : “Kids will be more likely to follow the role model player than follow the coach that’s harping on at them every day of the week” . Players often reported that coach motivation was critical, and “It would be virtually impossible (to do the injury prevention initiatives) without coach buy-in ”. Parents could play a critical role, particularly for concussion prevention strategies that rely on parents to purchase PPE. Parents’ education level, experiences (eg, contact sport or injury history) and attitudes may influence PPE adoption. Greater team resources and access to health/exercise/medical professionals may enhance D&I outcomes. However, the cost of accessing professionals and/or perceptions (eg, physiotherapist’s role is post-injury rehabilitation) may be barriers. A shared responsibility that fosters athlete, parent, coach, team, health and sport system leadership and culture appears critical. How are dissemination and implementation outcomes measured? D&I outcomes were mostly (55/67) reported in intervention groups only, mostly by athletes (33/67) or coaches/team personnel (23/67). Seven papers validated the coach/trainer D&I outcomes with field observations, and agreement ranged from 60% to 100%. Repeated measures were every session/2–3 time per week (22/67) or weekly (22/67), whereas cross-sectional assessments were typically at the end of the season (13/67). How much supervision and support? (56 experimental papers on training interventions) Most training interventions were incorporated into team practice (44/56), whereas 12/56 had a home/independent programme. Sixteen papers reported implementation supervision by study personnel (n=4 every session, n=6 weekly, n=2 periodic throughout season) or team trainers/health professionals (n=4, every session). Of the three papers evaluating the effect of supervision, all had better D&I outcomes than no supervision; however, only one was statistically significant. Nineteen papers included in-person or online/phone support delivered by study personnel to assist implementation (eg, troubleshoot and provide motivation). The effect of support on D&I outcomes was not evaluated. Discussion This scoping review synthesised the state of quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform current and future research and practice for the D&I of evidence-based injury prevention interventions for female/woman/girl athletes. The 220 included papers involved>4 00 000 participants, across multiple socio-ecological levels and 81 sports, and 49% were female/woman/girl athletes. The under-represented regions (Asia, Africa and South America), populations (eg, Para sport, sub-elite and children), D&I phases (sustainment), and study designs (D&I-focused trials) will direct future research on injury prevention D&I. Papers reported the level of D&I via >650 unique outcomes across the pre-implementation, implementation and sustainment phases, factors associated with D&I and current D&I strategies. Research targets: sociodemographic considerations The lack of research in Para sport, children, sub-elite and non-team sport athletes warrants future funding allocation and capacity building to better understand the unique implementation challenges in these settings. Understanding Para sport injury prevention needs is critical to inform intervention design and evaluation. Sociodemographic factors such as athlete and/or coach sex/gender or age, rurality, ethnic background, education level and school setting may influence implementation ( ) but require further research. Additional implementation barriers (eg, education access, funding opportunities and sports injury perceived importance relative to other health priorities) may exist in lower-income countries and/or more diverse cultural and religious contexts where gender norms, socioeconomic status, race and ethnicity intersect. Since few papers (22/220) used full D&I or hybrid effectiveness implementation type 2/3 designs, the most effective intervention/delivery characteristics (eg, type, education format/timing and level of supervision) remain unclear. Research targets: intervention type and dissemination and implementation outcomes The majority of papers were related to training interventions, and future research should explore the D&I of PPE and policy/rules/laws, which have been more extensively researched in male/men/boy’s contexts. Adoption was the most common D&I outcome assessed; however, it does not equate to how often or how well the intervention is used. More proximal D&I outcomes such as intervention adherence and its dimensions, including cumulative utilisation, utilisation frequency, utilisation fidelity and exercise fidelity, may facilitate dose–response analyses and inform essential programme components and potential adaptations. Practical targets: implementation strategies (who, what and how) Our practical recommendations are for female/women/girls, acknowledging data included mixed sex/gender studies (49% of athletes were female/woman/girl), and more targeted research is required. Fifty-five papers included only female/woman/girls ( ), and 36/165 mixed sex/gender papers disaggregated data ( ). Recommendations could be generalised to male/men/boys’ contexts, and potential female/women/girl-specific considerations are highlighted throughout. The positive perceptions and attitudes and moderate to high levels of adoption and cumulative utilisation identified in this review underpin our practical recommendations. Most D&I strategies included education and/or workshops either in-person (61%) or online (34%), typically delivered in pre-season (70%), by study personnel (63%), to athletes and/or coaches (96%). Few studies used deliverers beyond study personnel, and health/exercise/medical practitioners, coach/athlete educators, champions or technical directors should be involved in future implementation trials. Involving parents, team personnel and sport system administrators in education/workshops may share the responsibility, particularly in the context of under-resourced female/women/girls’ sport settings. Education usually includes lectures/information about injury risk, risk factors (often female sex-based), preventability and intervention efficacy. Given that injuries were perceived as a problem and preventative interventions beneficial, and several female-specific factors are non-modifiable (eg, anatomy), effort should shift to finding solutions to D&I barriers. Reduced lecturing style and more two-way discussions, self-practice, action planning and feedback with intervention users may enhance self-efficacy, adoption and sustained high-fidelity implementation. Pre-season education/workshops were mostly delivered in-person and may address the lack of transfer from better knowledge and positive intention to behaviour change. However, these strategies are resource-intensive, and only one of the two comparative RCTs reported superior D&I outcomes for a more supportive strategy. Although many RCTs had control groups with online materials, between-group D&I outcomes were rarely assessed, and few implementation cost-effectiveness studies exist, providing avenues for future research. In other fields (eg, psychiatry and nursing), online education minimised access and financial barriers with equivalent effectiveness (health/D&I outcomes) to in-person strategies. For PPE, online dissemination strategies may be sufficient, but the most effective platforms (eg, mobile apps, websites and social media) and formats (eg, video animations and infographics) remain unknown. Practical targets: implementation strategies (factors to consider) Practitioners may consider factors associated with D&I (previous injury experience, higher competition level and sport experience) to inform their strategies. Patient stories (ie, their injury experience and importance of prevention) could motivate others and optimise teammates, parents and support staff attitudes/intentions. Better D&I in higher competition levels may mean strategies are required to increase D&I in lower competition and less experienced athletes, for example, tailoring intervention content to amateur settings (eg, leaning into known facilitators for female/women/girls: fun, partner-based activities that are easy for coaches to learn and set up and adaptable to time/sport specific needs) and providing delivery support (eg, supervision and feedback). Female/women/girl athletes in lower competition levels may be more likely to engage in sport for social reasons; however, this should not disbar them from access to best practice injury prevention. Female-specific health factors (eg, breast tenderness and menstrual cycle/pelvic symptoms) may influence athlete participation (eg, reduced attendance or altered technique/performance in contact/impact activity due to symptoms). Raising coach awareness and providing strategies (eg, female health domain language they can use, environmental/personnel supports and technique/exercise modifications) that cater to needs specific to females/women/girls may enhance buy-in and uptake. However, some believe these approaches are unnecessarily progressive, and evaluation of sex/gender specific injury prevention interventions and D&I strategies is required. Practical targets: dissemination strategies Given that positive perceptions and attitudes among female/woman/girl athletes and coaches were associated with better D&I outcomes, pre-implementation initiatives to improve societal awareness and attitudes enhance implementation. Using social media campaigns to increase the uptake of evidence-based prevention interventions is effective (eg, immunology/vaccine uptake). Partnering with sporting organisations can help determine target markets, develop dissemination campaigns, while maintaining evidence-based messaging. Limitations This review only included publications in English, increasing the risk of language and publication bias. Sporting, education and government bodies may be employing injury prevention D&I initiatives without publishing their strategy or outcomes. The number of reviewers involved in screening and data extraction carries a small risk of error in data charting and interpretation. Under-representation of population groups (eg, Para sport, sub-elite and child athletes) limits the generalisability of findings. Conclusion This scoping review synthesised the state of quantitative and qualitative evidence to inform research and practice for the D&I of injury prevention interventions in female/woman/girl athletes. Perceptions and attitudes of coaches were mostly positive, whereas awareness, adoption and cumulative utilisation rates were moderate to high. Key facilitators of D&I include prior injury experience, higher competition level, greater sport experience and positive athlete and coach perceptions, attitudes, intentions and self-efficacy. Strategies to enhance D&I may include education and/or workshops in-person or online, delivered in pre-season by experts. There was limited attention on how well interventions are used or sustained and an unclear effect of supervision on D&I outcomes. Other critical gaps remain, and future research should prioritise under-represented regions (Asia, Africa and South America), populations (eg, studies on Para sport female/woman/girl only, sub-elite and children), D&I phases (sustainment) and study designs (D&I-focused trials). Most papers were focused on athletes and/or coaches. Engaging under-represented levels of the sport system (eg, parents, teachers, health/exercise/medical professionals, trainers and sport/school administrators) may help address the lower rates and understanding of fidelity and long-term sustainability and ultimately reduce injury risk in female/woman/girl athletes.
